name: Purple Rain (1984)
teaser: Prince wrote it as a guitar showcase and the film's concert scene is a real performance — the solo at the end is a single unedited take, and the song's gospel choir is the 'rain' made sound.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the full nine minutes with the solo — it's one unedited take. The song's genius is that the grief is the guitar; the lyrics are the weather.

name: Hotel California (1976)
teaser: The song's lyrics were written as a literal road trip gone wrong — the 'you can check out any time you like, but you can never leave' line is the song's thesis, and the famous dual guitar solo was improvised.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the dual guitar outro — two solos trading phrases. The song's genius is that the hotel is a metaphor you can't pin down; the ambiguity is the point.

name: Sweet Child o' Mine (1987)
teaser: The riff started as a string-skipping warm-up exercise that Slash called a joke — Axl wrote the lyrics in five minutes about his girlfriend, and the song became the band's biggest hit.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the intro and notice the 'joke' riff — the warm-up became the hook. The song's genius is that the guitar solo is a conversation with the vocal.

name: Creep (1992)
teaser: The band wrote the song's famous chord change accidentally — Thom Yorke's guitar swung between chords during a live show, and the audience's reaction made them keep it. It became their breakthrough despite being banned on some radio stations.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the quiet-loud structure — the verse is a whisper, the chorus is a scream. The song's genius is that the self-loathing is the hook.

name: Seven Nation Army (2003)
teaser: Jack White wrote the riff as a possible James Bond theme — the song's name came from his childhood mishearing of the Salvation Army. The riff has become a stadium chant worldwide.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the riff and notice it's a guitar pretending to be a bass. The song's genius is that the riff carries the whole song; the lyrics are the counter-melody.

name: Dancing Queen (1976)
teaser: Written for the Swedish king's wedding, the song's 'young and sweet, only seventeen' line was about a real 17-year-old who danced at a club ABBA visited — it's the only song ABBA wrote for a woman.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the piano intro and the key change — the song is engineered joy. The song's genius is that the disco beat is the 'dance' made literal.

name: Superstition (1972)
teaser: Stevie wrote the drum groove first — the 'superstition' lyrics came after, and the song's famous clavinet riff is played on a real Hohner Clavinet through a wah pedal.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the clavinet — it's the song's engine. The song's genius is that the groove is the thesis; the lyrics are the afterthought that made it a hit.

name: Comfortably Numb (1979)
teaser: The two guitar solos were recorded by two different guitarists (David Gilmour twice, years apart) — the song's lyrics are about Roger Waters' stage collapse and the doctor who injected him.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the two solos — the first is distant, the second is the climax. The song's genius is that the numbness is the narrator and the music is the feeling.

name: Don't Stop Believin' (1981)
teaser: The song flopped on release and became a hit years later through karaoke — the 'streetlight people' lyric is about real people in a real Detroit club, and the song's key change is its famous kick.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the key change before the final chorus — it's the song's ignition. The song's genius is that the 'believin'' is the instruction.

name: Crazy in Love (2003)
teaser: The song's famous horn sample was from a 1970 Chi-Lites record — producer Rich Harrison played it for Beyoncé and she danced to it on the spot. It launched her solo career.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the horn sample and the 'uh oh' — both are the hooks. The song's genius is that the horns are the chaos; the beat is the control.

name: I Will Survive (1978)
teaser: Written as the B-side after the label demanded a song about Gaynor's real injury — the 'survive' anthem became the first disco song to top the charts after disco's fall, a comeback in itself.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the string section and the spoken intro — the song is a speech. The song's genius is that the defiance is the hook; the 'survive' is the thesis.

name: London Calling (1979)
teaser: Written as a warning about the Thames flooding London — the band predicted the 'ice age' of climate change 40 years early, and the song's bassline is its most copied riff.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the bassline and the flood imagery — the warning is real. The song's genius is that the punk rage is a prophecy.

name: Bohemian Rhapsody (1975)
teaser: Freddie Mercury wrote most of it on the piano in his flat and the label refused to release a six-minute song with no chorus — it became one of the best-selling singles ever. The 'Galileo' backing vocals took three weeks to layer.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen with headphones and count the distinct sections — it's opera, ballad and hard rock in one track. Then listen for the multitracked 'Galileo' pile-up that takes the song to its peak.

name: Smells Like Teen Spirit (1991)
teaser: Kurt Cobain wrote the riff after mishearing a friend's slogan about a deodorant, and the band was sure it would flop — the music video's bored-mascot chaos made MTV viewers think the crowd was real.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the verse dynamics — it's the quiet-loud formula that ended an era of hair metal. Then watch the music video and notice the mascot's eyes: the apathy is the point.

name: Billie Jean (1982)
teaser: The bassline was built from a drum machine demo Quincy Jones wanted to cut, and the 'Not my lover' lyric was about a real fan's claim. The video broke MTV's color barrier in 1983.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the bassline first — it's the whole song's engine, and Jackson's vocal enters over it like a second instrument. Then count the empty beats in the intro: the tension is the hook.

name: Imagine (1971)
teaser: Lennon wrote it at his piano in Tittenhurst Park with Yoko watching, and the white room in the video is that actual house. It's the most-performed protest song of the 20th century without a single angry note.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the spare arrangement — just piano, voice and a string sweep that enters late. The radicalism is in how quiet it is; the 'no possessions' line lands because nothing is shouted.

name: Like a Rolling Stone (1965)
teaser: Dylan nearly shelved the six-minute draft as a novel fragment, and a session drummer's organ figure became the most famous riff in rock. It's the song that made pop lyrics literary.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the organ — it enters like a second voice answering every line. The song's question ('how does it feel?') is asked to the listener, not the subject.

name: Stairway to Heaven (1971)
teaser: The band kept it off singles for years so the album would sell, and the famous 'guitar store' ban was born from butchered covers. The recorder solo was played on a Mellotron, not real flutes.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen through headphones and track the volume arc — it's a quiet-to-loud journey in one song. The 'ooh-ooh' before the solo is the song's center of gravity.

name: Yesterday (1965)
teaser: Paul McCartney dreamed the melody and wrote the working title 'Scrambled Eggs' before settling on lyrics — it's the most-covered song ever, with over 2,200 recorded versions.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the string quartet — it was the first Beatles song to use classical instruments. The melody is so natural it feels inevitable; try to hear it without the violins and it loses half its sadness.

name: Hallelujah (1984)
teaser: Cohen wrote dozens of verses over five years — the song's famous 'secret chord' is a David reference, and it flopped on release before Jeff Buckley's 1994 cover made it immortal.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the Buckley version after the Cohen original and hear how the same words change meaning with a different voice. The song is about broken love disguised as scripture.

name: Respect (1967)
teaser: Written by Otis Redding as a man's plea, Aretha flipped the pronouns and demanded it — her version became a civil-rights and feminist anthem, and the 'R-E-S-P-E-C-T' spelling was her idea.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the spelling section — it's the song's thesis in letters. Then notice how the backing singers answer every line: the call-and-response is the argument.

name: Purple Haze (1967)
teaser: Hendrix said the lyric came from a dream about walking under the sea — the famous opening riff is a tritone, the 'devil's interval' banned in medieval church music.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the opening riff and hear the tritone — it's deliberately unsettling. Then notice how the solo bends the same interval back into melody.

name: What a Wonderful World (1967)
teaser: Satchmo recorded it at 66, and the label shelved it for a year — it only charted in the US after being used in a film. The song was written as an antidote to Vietnam-era cynicism.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to Armstrong's voice — recorded after his throat problems, it's the sound of a man who knows the world isn't wonderful and sings anyway. The trumpet at the end is his own instrument replying.

name: Thriller (1982)
teaser: The 14-minute video cost more than most films of the era and the song's famous Vincent Price rap was recorded in two takes — the werewolf howl is a real wolf recording.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the Vincent Price rap at the end — it's horror as pop. The song's bassline is the horror; the video just makes it visible.

name: Every Breath You Take (1983)
teaser: Sting wrote it in Jamaica after a divorce, and was horrified to realize people thought it romantic — it's a song about surveillance, not love, and it's one of the most-played songs ever.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the lyrics as a threat, not a promise — the stalker's logic is the song. The bass is the heartbeat; the song never resolves the tension.

name: My Heart Will Go On (1997)
teaser: James Horner wrote the theme secretly because the director hated songs in his films — Celine recorded it in one take, and the 'Titanic' flute is actually a synthesized penny whistle.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the synthesized whistle — it's not a real instrument. The song's melody was built from a demo Horner kept hidden; the director only heard it after the film was cut.

name: Shape of You (2017)
teaser: Sheeran wrote it about his girlfriend in 10 minutes, and the marimba riff was sampled from a demo he made with a toy. It became the most-streamed song on Spotify's history.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the marimba — it's the song's memory hook, and the verse's rhythmic switch ('the club isn't the best place') is the same riff in disguise. The song is a loop wearing a narrative.

name: Blinding Lights (2019)
teaser: The song's 80s synth-pop sound made it the most-streamed song in Spotify history — it spent a record 90 weeks on the Billboard Hot 100. Its neon video was filmed in a parking garage in a single night.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the drum machine and the synth arpeggio — they're pure 1980s. The song's loneliness is hidden under the dance beat; the 'I can't see clearly' line is literal in the video.

name: Old Town Road (2019)
teaser: Made with a $30 beat from a teenager on YouTube, the song was removed from the country charts and Billy Ray Cyrus joined a remix — it spent 19 weeks at #1, a record.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the banjo over the trap beat — the genre clash is the point. The song's viral life is its real story; the remix with Cyrus is the chapter that made it history.

name: Royals (2013)
teaser: Lorde wrote the hook after seeing a photo of a Royals baseball cap, and the label nearly cut the track — the minimal production was the 16-year-old's rebellion against opulent pop.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for what's NOT there — the song has almost no bass and no chorus explosion. The minimalism is the message: luxury is the absence of need.

name: Rolling in the Deep (2010)
teaser: Adele wrote it in 10 minutes after a breakup, and the stomping percussion was recorded by stamping on a floor — the 'gonna make you love me' threat is the whole song.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the stomp — it's a foot on a wooden floor, and it IS the beat. The song's anger is in the restraint; the key change at the end is a door slamming.

name: Uptown Funk (2014)
teaser: The song's Minneapolis-funk sound made it one of the best-selling singles ever — it spent 14 weeks at No. 1. Its video, full of disco suits, was a homage to 80s nightlife.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the bassline — it's a direct descendant of 1970s funk. The song's genius is that it sounds improvised but every fill is placed; count the horn stabs.

name: Wonderwall (1995)
teaser: Noel Gallagher has said the song was written about 'an imaginary friend who's gonna come and save you from yourself' — he's also called the lyric meaningless. It became the Britpop era's defining anthem.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the 'maybe' that starts the chorus — it's the song's engine. The song is a promise that never lands; the narrator doesn't know if the wall will break either.

name: Lose Yourself (2002)
teaser: The song was written for the film 8 Mile and became the first rap song to win the Oscar for Best Original Song. Eminem wrote it in a single take in the studio bathroom.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the opening — the record scratch and the first verse are a single breath. The song's anxiety is the point: the palm-sweat moment is the song.

name: Sicko Mode (2018)
teaser: The song is three beats stitched together with no chorus — it was literally made in the studio with producer switch-ups mid-session, and the beat changes are the hook.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the beat switches — there are three, and each one resets the song's momentum. The song's structure is its subject: chaos as composition.

name: Gangnam Style (2012)
teaser: The first YouTube video to pass a billion views — PSY's 'horse dance' was based on his own actual bad dancing, and the lyrics mock Seoul's wealthy Gangnam district.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the video and notice the satire — the 'rich' scenes are all absurd. The song's joke is that the dancer is neither rich nor cool; the dance is the punchline.

name: Dynamite (2020)
teaser: The first all-Korean-group song to debut at #1 on the Hot 100 — the disco-pop track was released during lockdown and its music video's retro styling is a direct 1970s homage.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the disco strings and the handclaps — the 1970s references are precise. The song's joy is political: a Korean group singing 'light it up like dynamite' in English was a statement.

name: Gangsta's Paradise (1995)
teaser: The song's chorus was adapted from Stevie Wonder's 'Pastime Paradise' — and the video, from the film Dangerous Minds, made it one of the biggest hits of the decade. It was the best-selling single of 1995 worldwide.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the Stevie Wonder sample — the choir underneath is his original. The song's power is the contrast between the serene sample and the violent verses.

name: Africa (1982)
teaser: The band wrote it as a joke about Westerners romanticizing Africa, and the song's famous backing vocals took hours to record — it became a meme decades later, loved for being sincere.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the kalimba (thumb piano) — it's the song's signature sound, played by the keyboardist who'd never touched one before. The song's earnestness is why the meme works.

name: I Will Always Love You (1973)
teaser: Dolly wrote it as a farewell to her mentor Porter Wagoner and refused to sell the publishing — Whitney's 1992 cover made it one of the best-selling singles ever, and Dolly kept her rights.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to Dolly's original first — it's a country ballad, not a power anthem. Then hear Whitney's a cappella opening: the song was always about the space between two people.

name: Jolene (1973)
teaser: The song's melody was inspired by a real girl who flirted with her husband, and the name came from a young fan — Dolly wrote it in one afternoon and the 'pleading' vocal is a country masterclass.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the desperation in the first verse — the narrator doesn't ask, she begs. The song's genius is that Jolene is never described as evil; she's just beautiful, and that's enough.

name: Take On Me (1985)
teaser: The song charted in three different decades and its rotoscope animation video was a technical breakthrough — the band re-recorded it four times over three years before it hit.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the synth riff — it's one of the most recognizable in pop. The video's sketch-to-real transition is the song made visual: the pencil world is the synth world.

name: Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This) (1983)
teaser: The song was built on a $20 drum machine loop and Annie Lennox's iconic video look was a last-minute decision — the band was broke and the label nearly cut them.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the drum machine — it's the whole song's skeleton, and the bassline enters like a third voice. The video's gender-play is the song's real subject: identity as costume.

name: Video Games (2011)
teaser: Made on a laptop in a bedroom and uploaded to YouTube, the song's lo-fi production launched a million imitators — the vintage-film aesthetic was also homemade.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the film-sound effects under the vocals — the song was literally scored like a movie. The 'heaven is a place on earth' sample is the ghost in the machine.

name: Somebody That I Used to Know (2011)
teaser: The song's duet structure was inspired by a breakup, and the 'body paint' music video is one continuous shot — the artist spent years away from music after its success.

exploreAction.targetName: Somebody That I Used to Know (2011)
exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the two voices — they never sing together, which IS the song. The 'now you're just somebody' line is the thesis; the video's paint makes it literal.

name: Hey Ya! (2003)
teaser: André 3000 wrote the song as a Beatles-inspired collage — the verses are in a different tempo from the chorus, and the song famously ends with an outro that feels like the band falling apart. It's been called one of the greatest pop songs ever.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the key change at the end — it's the song's confession. The funk is the mask; the lyrics are a relationship falling apart in a club.

name: Happy (2013)
teaser: The song was written for a film and rejected, then released as a single — the 24-hour music video was shot in 24 locations with real people dancing, and the claps were recorded in the studio.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the claps — they're the song's heartbeat, recorded by Pharrell's own hands. The song's simplicity is the craft; there's no bridge, just joy.

name: Can't Stop the Feeling! (2016)
teaser: Written for a Trolls movie, the song's disco revival made it the biggest-selling single of 2016 — the 'happy' is engineered, which is exactly the point. Can't Stop the Feeling!

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the falsetto 'nothing can stop me' — it's the song's peak, and it arrives without a build. The song is pure chemical joy; the disco strings are the prescription.

name: Toxic (2003)
teaser: The song's Bollywood strings and its 'too toxic' chorus made it a critical favorite — it's often ranked among the greatest pop songs ever. The video, with Britney as a spy, is a classic.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the Bollywood strings — they're the song's secret weapon. The song's danger is in the beat; the lyrics are the warning label.

name: Umbrella (2007)
teaser: The song's 'ella, ella' hook was almost rejected by Rihanna's label — it became her first global No. 1 and one of the best-selling digital singles of its time. The raindrop intro is iconic.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the 'ella ella' hook — it's the song's memory engine, and the beat's heartbeat is the rain. The song's promise ('under my umbrella') is the whole story.

name: Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It) (2008)
teaser: The video's dance was choreographed to look like two backup dancers — Beyoncé performed it on a bare soundstage. The song's message about commitment became a cultural moment.

exploreAction.targetName: Single Ladies (Put a Ring on It) (2008)
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the video and count the three dancers — the precision is the performance. The song's demand is its power: the ring is the argument.

name: Havana (2017)
teaser: The song's 'Havana, ooh na-na' hook was improvised in the studio, and the video's old-movie aesthetic hides a twist — the song's Cuba longing is real, but the ending is a joke.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the trumpet — it's the song's soul, played by a real session musician. The song is a love letter to a city the singer barely knew; that's the ache.

name: Despacito (2017)
teaser: The reggaeton hit with Justin Bieber's remix became the most-streamed song of all time at the time — its 'despacito' chorus made Spanish-language pop mainstream.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the original, not the remix — the Spanish phrasing is the song's architecture. The 'despacito' hook is the whole song in one word.

name: Waka Waka (This Time for Africa) (2010)
teaser: Written for the 2010 World Cup, the song's chorus samples a 1980s Cameroonian hit — the dance moves in the video are real African dances.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the sampled Cameroonian guitar — the song is a translation. The 'Waka Waka' hook is a real Tsonga phrase meaning 'do it do it'.

name: Firework (2010)
teaser: Perry wrote it after reading Jack Kerouac's On the Road — the song's 'firework' metaphor was inspired by a real comment from a fan who felt invisible.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the key change before the final chorus — it's the song's ignition. The song's pep talk is engineered, but the engineering is the craft.

name: Born This Way (2011)
teaser: Gaga wrote it as a direct answer to the bullying she survived in school — the song's 'born this way' became a queer anthem and the music video is a birth-to-rebirth allegory.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the spoken opening — it's a sermon, not a verse. The song's radicalism is that it refuses to argue: the self is the fact.

name: All Too Well (2012)
teaser: The 10-minute version's release in 2021 broke records — the song's 'scarf' lyric is famously autobiographical, and the song's real subject is the memory of a memory.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the scarf — it's the song's emotional anchor, and it never comes back. The song's genius is that the narrator can't stop telling the story she's telling.

name: Circles (2019)
teaser: The song's mellow pop-rap sound became one of the biggest hits of the decade — it spent a record-breaking time on the charts and its video was a western comedy.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the circle — the progression returns to the start, and the song never resolves. The song's trap is that you can't leave a loop you're in.

name: Snooze (2022)
teaser: SZA wrote it about being so in love she can't sleep — the song's 'snooze' is both the state and the excuse, and the album it came from won Album of the Year.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the falsetto 'I'll touch you in the morning' — the promise is the song's core. The production's warmth is the love; the lyrics are the anxiety.

name: Kill Bill (2022)
teaser: The song's revenge fantasy samples a 1980s R&B hit and the video's bridal-gore aesthetic made it a viral moment — the humor is the point, the violence is the joke.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the sampled Diana Ross hook — the sweetness is the contrast. The song's confession ('I might kill my ex') is funny precisely because it's sung so gently.

name: (I Can't Get No) Satisfaction (1965)
teaser: Keith Richards wrote the riff in his sleep and recorded it on a cassette by his bed; the track's raw fuzz tone came from a Gibson Maestro fuzz pedal. It became the Stones' first American No. 1.

exploreAction.targetName: (I Can't Get No) Satisfaction (1965) by The Rolling Stones
exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the fuzz-guitar riff entering after the drum count-in — it was meant as a temporary placeholder Keith taped overnight.

name: A Change Is Gonna Come (1964)
teaser: Cooke wrote it after being turned away from a whites-only motel in Louisiana. He died three weeks before it was released, and it grew into the civil-rights movement's anthem.

exploreAction.targetName: A Change Is Gonna Come (1964) by Sam Cooke
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to how the orchestral arrangement swells under the last verse — the hope and exhaustion in one voice.

name: My Generation (1965)
teaser: Roger Daltrey's stutter was a stammering protest against older generations; John Entwistle's bass solo was one of the first in rock. It peaked at No. 2 in the UK because the BBC thought the stutter mocked disabled people.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen past the stutter to Entwistle's bass solo — the moment the bass stops keeping time and starts leading.

name: Good Vibrations (1966)
teaser: Brian Wilson called it a 'pocket symphony' — it was built from hundreds of tape splices recorded in four studios over six months and was the most expensive single of its era, around $50,000. It still topped the charts.

exploreAction.targetName: Good Vibrations (1966) by The Beach Boys
exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the cello and the theremin — and count how many distinct 'sections' the song has; it's more a collage than a verse-chorus song.

name: God Only Knows (1966)
teaser: Paul McCartney has called it the greatest song ever written. It opens with a French horn and a harpsichord, and its chord changes wander where pop songs weren't supposed to go.

exploreAction.targetName: God Only Knows (1966) by The Beach Boys
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the bass line — it moves in counterpoint to the melody, almost like a second song underneath.

name: A Day in the Life (1967)
teaser: The song is two Lennon and McCartney fragments stitched together, and the orchestral crescendos were recorded with the orchestra improvising upward. The final piano chord rings for over 40 seconds.

exploreAction.targetName: A Day in the Life (1967) by The Beatles
exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the moment the alarm clock rings, then follow the 24-bar orchestral build — count how long the final chord actually rings.

name: Strawberry Fields Forever (1967)
teaser: The released version splices two takes recorded in different keys and tempos — the edit point is audible right after the line 'let me take you down'. The slowed-down tape makes Lennon's voice sound dreamier than he sang it.

exploreAction.targetName: Strawberry Fields Forever (1967) by The Beatles
exploreAction.instruction: Listen at the edit seam after the first chorus — you can hear the take change mid-word.

name: Light My Fire (1967)
teaser: The single was cut down from over seven minutes, which infuriated Jim Morrison — he and the band played the full version on The Ed Sullivan Show anyway. Ray Manzarek's organ solo was the song's centerpiece.

exploreAction.targetName: Light My Fire (1967) by The Doors
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to Manzarek's organ solo — it trades lines with Robby Krieger's guitar as if they're having a conversation.

name: Sunshine of Your Love (1967)
teaser: Jack Bruce wrote the riff after jamming with Jimi Hendrix, and the melody was sketched out on bass. Eric Clapton's wah-wah-less solo made it the blueprint for hard rock.

exploreAction.targetName: Sunshine of Your Love (1967) by Cream
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the riff under the solo — it never stops, anchoring everything Bruce and Clapton play over it.

name: All Along the Watchtower (1968)
teaser: Bob Dylan wrote it, but Hendrix's version — with its stabbing guitar and slower pace — is the one everyone knows. Dylan later said Hendrix 'found it' and he's been performing it Hendrix's way ever since.

exploreAction.targetName: All Along the Watchtower (1968) by Jimi Hendrix
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to how Hendrix spaces the guitar stabs around the vocals — silence is part of the arrangement.

name: Sympathy for the Devil (1968)
teaser: The driving rhythm came from Brazilian samba — Keith Richards had been listening to Bateria de escola de samba records. The song needed an extra verse after a first take fell apart; the final version was the fourth take.

exploreAction.targetName: Sympathy for the Devil (1968) by The Rolling Stones
exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the samba groove under the chaos — and for the backing vocals chanting in the background of the final section.

name: Proud Mary (1969)
teaser: John Fogerty wrote it after leaving the Army, where the 'proud Mary' was the nickname of a riverboat. The famous slow-fast-slow structure came from a live-show arrangement the band fell into.

exploreAction.targetName: Proud Mary (1969) by Creedence Clearwater Revival
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the gear change when the intro drops into the shuffle — notice how the whole band locks in at once.

name: Suzanne (1967)
teaser: Cohen wrote it about Suzanne Verdal, a real Montreal woman, and the 'tea and oranges' are true — she served him exactly that. The song's religious imagery started as a poem before it had music.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the spoken cadence — Cohen talks the verses like poetry before the chorus lifts.

name: The Sound of Silence (1965)
teaser: The acoustic version flopped, then producer Tom Wilson overdubbed electric guitars and drums without telling the duo — that version became a No. 1 hit and launched the folk-rock boom.

exploreAction.targetName: The Sound of Silence (1965) by Simon & Garfunkel
exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the electric guitar entering under the second verse — it's a different song than the one they wrote.

name: Mr. Tambourine Man (1965)
teaser: Bob Dylan wrote it, but the Byrds' 12-string Rickenbacker version is what made folk-rock a genre. The band's first recording was almost scrapped — only Roger McGuinn played on the released single.

exploreAction.targetName: Mr. Tambourine Man (1965) by The Byrds
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the jangle of the 12-string — it was the sound every other band tried to copy that year.

name: Waterloo Sunset (1967)
teaser: Ray Davies wrote it watching the crowds cross Waterloo Bridge in London; the 'terry and julie' of the lyric were his sister and her boyfriend. It's been called the most beautiful song about London ever written.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to how the two guitar lines interlock — Davies said the sound of the song is the sound of a London afternoon.

name: Paint It Black (1966)
teaser: Brian Jones played the sitar — one of the first times a sitar anchored a rock single, months before the Beatles' 'Norwegian Wood'. The song's darkness was a deliberate turn from the band's pop hits.

exploreAction.targetName: Paint It Black (1966) by The Rolling Stones
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the sitar doubling the guitar riff — it gives the minor-key march its eastern, brooding color.

name: Eleanor Rigby (1966)
teaser: The song has no guitars — just a string octet. The name Eleanor Rigby came from a gravestone Paul McCartney spotted in a Liverpool cemetery; the real Eleanor Rigby is buried there.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the strings alone — the song is a mini-movie scored for double quartet, with the vocals as the only 'band'.

name: Hey Jude (1968)
teaser: It was written as 'Hey Jules' to comfort Julian Lennon during his parents' divorce. At over seven minutes it was the longest No. 1 single of its time, and the 'na na na' coda lasts nearly four minutes.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to how the four-minute singalong builds — the band joins in stages until the whole thing is one giant refrain.

name: Space Oddity (1969)
teaser: Released five days before Apollo 11 launched, it tells of Major Tom floating in his tin can. The BBC used it during their moon-landing coverage, cementing the song's link to the space race.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the countdown and the separation of Major Tom from Ground Control — the loneliness is in the echo and the gaps.

name: Piece of My Heart (1968)
teaser: Janis Joplin's screaming rendition is the famous one, but Erma Franklin — Aretha's sister — recorded the original two years earlier. Joplin's version turned the soul ballad into a rock shriek.
byline: Big Brother and the Holding Company

exploreAction.targetName: Piece of My Heart (1968) by Big Brother and the Holding Company
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to Joplin's voice cracking on the repeated 'take it' — that raggedness is the whole point.

name: California Dreamin' (1965)
teaser: John Phillips wrote it one freezing New York winter, dreaming of LA's warmth. The flute line was an afterthought that became the song's signature, and the arrangement was built around a slowed-down bossa-nova rhythm.

exploreAction.targetName: California Dreamin' (1965) by The Mamas & the Papas
exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the flute melody — it enters after the first chorus and quietly takes over the song.

name: Brown Eyed Girl (1967)
teaser: The original lyric was 'brown skinned girl' — a love song to an interracial relationship — and the label made him change it. The recording happened in a few takes with session musicians.

exploreAction.targetName: Brown Eyed Girl (1967) by Van Morrison
exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the tambourine and the abrupt key change after the second chorus — the song jumps keys like a memory jumping years.

name: White Rabbit (1967)
teaser: Grace Slick wrote it with Alice in Wonderland references — the hook 'feed your head' pointed at psychedelics. The bolero-style crescendo builds from a whisper to a full-band roar.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to how the song keeps getting louder — the Spanish march rhythm ratchets the tension until the final scream.

name: Born to Be Wild (1968)
teaser: The lyric 'heavy metal thunder' is widely credited as the first use of the phrase 'heavy metal' in a rock song. The song's rumble came from an actual motorcycle engine revved in the studio.

exploreAction.targetName: Born to Be Wild (1968) by Steppenwolf
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the engine revving at the start — before a single guitar note, the song already sounds like a bike.

name: Gimme Shelter (1969)
teaser: Merry Clayton was woken at midnight to sing the backing vocal; her voice cracks on 'murder' and the tape kept the take. Days later she was in a car accident that put her in a wheelchair, lending the lyric a chilling edge.

exploreAction.targetName: Gimme Shelter (1969) by The Rolling Stones
exploreAction.instruction: Listen for Clayton's voice cracking on the word 'murder' — the band kept that imperfect, terrified take.

name: Suspicious Minds (1969)
teaser: It was Elvis's 18th and final American No. 1. Producer Chips Moman recorded it in Memphis against Elvis's label's wishes, and the famous fade-out-fade-back-in ending was Moman's idea to keep the song from ending.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the ending that won't end — the song fades out, then fades back in, as if it refuses to let go.

name: You Really Got Me (1964)
teaser: The distorted power-chord riff was born when Dave Davies slashed his amp's speaker cone with a razor and pushed it to the brink. That two-note riff is considered a birth certificate of heavy metal.

exploreAction.targetName: You Really Got Me (1964) by The Kinks
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to how raw the guitar sounds — compare it to the clean pop records around it; it's a different species.

name: (Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay (1968)
teaser: Redding wrote it while houseboating in Sausalito and recorded it three days before his plane crash; the whistling outro came from him forgetting the lyrics and improvising. It became his only No. 1.

exploreAction.targetName: (Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay (1968) by Otis Redding
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the whistling at the end — a placeholder that became one of the most famous outros in soul.

name: In the Midnight Hour (1965)
teaser: Steve Cropper wrote the rhythm around a dance move: Pickett showed him the 'wait-a-minute' step where dancers pause on the beat. The famous bass line drops out on that pause.

exploreAction.targetName: In the Midnight Hour (1965) by Wilson Pickett
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the bass dropping out on the beat — that silence is the dance step made into music.

name: My Girl (1964)
teaser: Smokey Robinson wrote it in under an hour after David Ruffin joined the group, and the famous opening bass line was played by Motown's James Jamerson. The guitar riff was an afterthought that became iconic.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the bass intro — four notes that tell you the whole song before a single word is sung.

name: For What It's Worth (1966)
teaser: Stephen Stills wrote it about the Sunset Strip curfew riots in Los Angeles — 'Stop, hey what's that sound' was the sound of police lines. It was recorded in three takes and released two weeks later.

exploreAction.targetName: For What It's Worth (1966) by Buffalo Springfield
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the claps and the jangly guitar lock into the marching rhythm — the song walks like the protest it describes.

name: These Boots Are Made for Walkin' (1966)
teaser: Lee Hazlewood wrote it and the menacing bass 'walk' line drove the whole arrangement. The song was a response to the era's male pop stars — Sinatra's delivery turned it into a quiet threat.

exploreAction.targetName: These Boots Are Made for Walkin' (1966) by Nancy Sinatra
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the bass line that literally walks — and to how little the song needs: a bass, a shuffle, and a stare.

name: Nights in White Satin (1967)
teaser: It was the centerpiece of Days of Future Passed, recorded with the London Festival Orchestra — one of the first rock albums built around a symphony. The poem 'Late Lament' is recited over the final section.

exploreAction.targetName: Nights in White Satin (1967) by The Moody Blues
exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the orchestral swell and the spoken poem at the end — the song turns into something closer to film music.

name: A Whiter Shade of Pale (1967)
teaser: The organ melody was borrowed from Bach's 'Air on a G String', and the surreal lyrics were written by Keith Reid in the back of a van. It sold over ten million copies worldwide.

exploreAction.targetName: A Whiter Shade of Pale (1967) by Procol Harum
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the Bach-inspired organ line — the song is a hymn that never quite explains its own words.

name: Reach Out I'll Be There (1966)
teaser: Written by Motown's Holland-Dozier-Holland, it built on a single tambourine figure and Levi Stubbs' desperate vocal. It was Motown's first song to be a genuine international rock-stadium anthem.

exploreAction.targetName: Reach Out I'll Be There (1966) by The Four Tops
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the tambourine — one steady sixteenth-note pulse that never stops, holding the whole song together.

name: River Deep – Mountain High (1966)
teaser: Phil Spector poured everything into it and called it his best work, but it flopped in America — his label reportedly bought back the master. It was a huge hit in the UK instead.

exploreAction.targetName: River Deep – Mountain High (1966) by Ike & Tina Turner
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the wall of sound — dozens of instruments playing at once, with Tina's voice climbing over the top.

name: Be My Baby (1963)
teaser: The archetypal Phil Spector wall-of-sound record — Hal Blaine's four-beat drum intro is one of the most imitated in pop. Ronnie Spector's voice was recorded in a stairwell for extra echo.

exploreAction.targetName: Be My Baby (1963) by The Ronettes
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the drum intro alone — it's been copied by every band since; notice how it returns before each chorus.

name: You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin' (1964)
teaser: At nearly four minutes it was considered too long for radio — Spector and the songwriters refused to cut it, and it became the most-played song of the 20th century on American radio.

exploreAction.targetName: You've Lost That Lovin' Feelin' (1964) by The Righteous Brothers
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to how the song builds in waves — Spector kept adding layers until the last chorus is huge.

name: Unchained Melody (1965)
teaser: It was written for the 1955 film Unchained — the 'unchained' melody of a prisoner. Bobby Hatfield's soaring solo take is the famous version; the song has been recorded over 1,500 times.

exploreAction.targetName: Unchained Melody (1965) by The Righteous Brothers
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to Hatfield's long, held notes on 'I need your love' — he sang the whole thing in one pass.

name: I Heard It Through the Grapevine (1968)
teaser: Gladys Knight & the Pips charted first with it, but Marvin Gaye's brooding take became Motown's biggest-selling single ever. The wah-wah guitar and low organ give it an unease no other version has.

exploreAction.targetName: I Heard It Through the Grapevine (1968) by Marvin Gaye
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the organ and wah-wah underneath — the song sounds paranoid before the story even starts.

name: Ain't No Mountain High Enough (1967)
teaser: Ashford & Simpson wrote it as a pop-soul duet; Marvin Gaye and Tammi Terrell were label partners, and Tammi was already battling the illness that ended her career the next year.

exploreAction.targetName: Ain't No Mountain High Enough (1967) by Marvin Gaye & Tammi Terrell
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the two voices trade lines — the song is a duet where each singer answers the other's promise.

name: The Tracks of My Tears (1965)
teaser: Robinson wrote the lyric about hiding heartbreak behind a smile — the 'tracks of my tears' are the mascara lines. The guitar intro by Marv Tarplin became one of Motown's most famous openings.

exploreAction.targetName: The Tracks of My Tears (1965) by Smokey Robinson & the Miracles
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the guitar intro and the way the melody descends — sadness that arrives already dressed up.

name: Dancing in the Street (1964)
teaser: Written by Marvin Gaye, Mickey Stevenson and Ivy Jo Hunter, it started as a song about dancing in cities across America — and got adopted by protest movements as an anthem. It has been covered by everyone from Van Halen to Bowie and Jagger.

exploreAction.targetName: Dancing in the Street (1964) by Martha and the Vandellas
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the hand-claps and the brass — a call to arms disguised as a dance record.

name: Stand by Me (1961)
teaser: King based it on the gospel hymn 'Stand By Me' and nearly passed on recording it. Its famous bass line was adapted from another song's intro — and it's been covered by over 400 artists.

exploreAction.targetName: Stand by Me (1961) by Ben E. King
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the bass line under the whole song — it never stops, and it's the real hook.

name: Twist and Shout (1963)
teaser: The Beatles recorded it in a single take at the very end of their first album session, when John Lennon's throat was already raw — the rasp is real exhaustion. It's an Isley Brothers song that the Beatles made iconic.

exploreAction.targetName: Twist and Shout (1963) by The Beatles
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to Lennon's voice shredding on the last chorus — one take, no overdub possible.

name: I Want to Hold Your Hand (1963)
teaser: It was the record that broke the Beatles in America — the first song of theirs to top the US chart. The 'yeah yeah yeah' hook was mocked by critics and imitated by every band that followed.

exploreAction.targetName: I Want to Hold Your Hand (1963) by The Beatles
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the opening chord — it arrives with no intro at all, just a declaration.

name: She Loves You (1963)
teaser: It became the fastest-selling single in UK history at the time, moving over a million copies in under a month. The 'yeah yeah yeah' call-and-response changed how pop songs ended.

exploreAction.targetName: She Loves You (1963) by The Beatles
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the outro — the song fades on the band shouting 'yeah' back at itself, an idea nobody had tried.

name: All You Need Is Love (1967)
teaser: It was performed live on Our World, the first global satellite television broadcast, watched by an estimated 400 million people. The band wrote and rehearsed it in two weeks for that one show.

exploreAction.targetName: All You Need Is Love (1967) by The Beatles
exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the orchestral instruments and crowd noise bleeding in — the broadcast is part of the recording.

name: Come Together (1969)
teaser: Lennon wrote it as a campaign song for Timothy Leary's California governor run, then rewrote it with a swampy, bluesy groove. The drum intro and the 'shoot me' refrain survived the rewrite.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the way Lennon's voice slurs the syllables — the words ride the beat instead of the other way around.

name: Something (1969)
teaser: George Harrison's first Beatles A-side; Frank Sinatra called it 'the greatest love song of the past 50 years'. The demo was written on piano during the White Album sessions.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the guitar solo — it's a quiet, bent-note statement that never raises its voice.

name: Wichita Lineman (1968)
teaser: Jimmy Webb wrote it in a parking lot after seeing a lone lineman on a pole — the 'lineman for the county' whose lonely phone line inspired one of the first country-pop crossover hits. Webb has called it 'the first existential country song'.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the eerie, almost cinematic strings behind Campbell's voice — loneliness rendered as a telephone wire.

name: MacArthur Park (1968)
teaser: Jimmy Webb's seven-minute epic about a love affair ending in a park — 'someone left the cake out in the rain'. The actor Richard Harris sang it, and the version became a worldwide hit.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the way the song keeps shifting time signatures — it's a short film in music.

name: The Weight (1968)
teaser: Robbie Robertson wrote it after the band retreated to a pink house in Woodstock, and the song's 'take a load off Fanny' is pure gospel-style storytelling. It's been called a fable of American kindness and duty.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the call-and-response vocals — the song is a town full of voices answering each other.

name: Voodoo Child (Slight Return) (1968)
teaser: It was improvised on the spot while filming a BBC documentary — the band had been playing the slower 'Voodoo Chile' and Hendrix launched into this version unprompted. It became his signature riff.

exploreAction.targetName: Voodoo Child (Slight Return) (1968) by Jimi Hendrix
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the opening riff — it was made up in that exact moment, in front of the cameras.

name: Crosstown Traffic (1968)
teaser: The horn-like sound in the intro is Hendrix playing a kazoo made of a comb and paper through the microphone. It's the closest the album Electric Ladyland gets to a straight pop song.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the kazoo — it's pretending to be a horn section, and it's completely improvised.

name: American Pie (1971)
teaser: The 'day the music died' refers to the 1959 plane crash that killed Buddy Holly, Ritchie Valens and the Big Bopper. At over eight minutes, radio stations refused to play the full version at first.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to how the chorus keeps returning with more force each time — the song is a decade of American music in one melody.

name: Rocket Man (1972)
teaser: Bernie Taupin's lyric was inspired by Ray Bradbury's story 'The Rocket Man', about an astronaut for whom space is just a job. Elton's melody was written in under an hour.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the song's loneliness — the rocket man isn't heroic, he's homesick.

name: Baba O'Riley (1971)
teaser: The pulsing synth loop came from a Lowrey Berkshire organ programmed to cycle patterns — the band simply recorded it and played over it. The song is named after spiritual teacher Meher Baba and composer Terry Riley.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the synthesized 'violin' loop — it was made on a home organ, years before synths were standard.

name: Won't Get Fooled Again (1971)
teaser: Keith Moon's drumming on the song's second half was recorded in one unedited pass; the final 'meet the new boss, same as the old boss' scream is one of rock's great catharses.

exploreAction.targetName: Won't Get Fooled Again (1971) by The Who
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the drum break that stops the song cold before the final verse — Moon holds it together by almost falling apart.

name: Dream On (1973)
teaser: Steven Tyler wrote the lyrics when he was 17, and the song's verse is built on the same four chords as a classical piece — a Pachelbel-style progression. It took years to chart.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the way the song keeps climbing in key — every chorus is higher than the last.

name: Born to Run (1975)
teaser: Springsteen spent six months layering the sound — Roy Bittan's piano, Clarence Clemons' sax and a wall of guitars — to capture the teenage rush of escaping a dead-end town. The title came to him in a dream.

exploreAction.targetName: Born to Run (1975) by Bruce Springsteen
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the opening — the keyboard and guitar hit together like a car engine turning over.

name: Thunder Road (1975)
teaser: The title comes from a 1958 Robert Mitchum film, and the opening harmonica and slamming screen door set the whole album's mood. The 'Mary' of the song was a recurring character in Springsteen's early lyrics.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the harmonica fade-in before the band enters — it's the sound of a small town at dawn.

name: Highway to Hell (1979)
teaser: The title came from a tour route: the band's manager joked their never-ending Australian touring schedule was 'the highway to hell'. It became Bon Scott's final album with the band before his death.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the relentless chug of the riff — it's a road song that never lets off the gas.

name: T.N.T. (1975)
teaser: The 'Oi! Oi! Oi!' chant came from a hockey crowd — the band heard it at a game and stole it for the chorus. The song has outlived the original 1975 single and remains a stadium staple.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to how the chorus is just one chord held forever with the band yelling over it — simplicity as power.

name: Whole Lotta Love (1969)
teaser: The famous riff was a reworking of a Muddy Waters blues line — the band credited it to Willie Dixon after a lawsuit. The psychedelic middle section with theremin was Robert Plant's idea.

exploreAction.targetName: Whole Lotta Love (1969) by Led Zeppelin
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the theremin swooping through the middle — the song falls apart into noise and then rebuilds itself.

name: Immigrant Song (1970)
teaser: Written after a gig in Iceland, it's about Viking conquest — 'we come from the land of the ice and snow'. Robert Plant's wail was recorded in one take with the band playing live.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to Plant's opening scream — it was cut live in the studio with the full band, no overdub.

name: Black Dog (1971)
teaser: The a cappella opening and the shifting time signatures made it nearly impossible to dance to — the band wanted a song that would confuse club DJs. The title came from a black labrador that wandered the studio.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the way the band drops out — the vocals carry alone before the riff slams back in.

name: Kashmir (1975)
teaser: Jimmy Page wrote the riff in an open DADGAD tuning while the band toured Morocco, and the song's marching strings were overdubbed later. It remains one of the most orchestral things rock has ever done.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the strings and the odd half-time feel — the song marches like a caravan, not a rock band.

name: Free Bird (1973)
teaser: The nine-minute epic's famous triple-guitar solo was improvised in the studio after the band decided the song needed a long ending. 'Free bird' became the cry audiences yelled at every concert.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the last three minutes — three guitars trading solos that keep getting louder and faster.

name: Sweet Home Alabama (1974)
teaser: It was a response to Neil Young's 'Southern Man' — Ronnie Van Zant sang 'I hope Neil Young will remember'. Despite the feud rumors, the two were friends.

exploreAction.targetName: Sweet Home Alabama (1974) by Lynyrd Skynyrd
exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the guitar intro's three-note hook — and the backing 'Alabama' chant that answers every line.

name: Dreams (1977)
teaser: Stevie Nicks wrote it in about ten minutes in a closet at the Record Plant studios, sitting on a cushion, while the rest of the band worked on other songs. It became the band's only US No. 1.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the stillness — Mick Fleetwood's drum pattern and the bass leave room for Nicks' voice to float.

name: Go Your Own Way (1977)
teaser: Lindsey Buckingham wrote it about his split from Stevie Nicks — and Nicks sang backing vocals on the song that told her to leave. The ending guitar riff was his goodbye.

exploreAction.targetName: Go Your Own Way (1977) by Fleetwood Mac
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to how raw the vocal is on 'you can go your own way' — the band kept the pain in the take.

name: The Chain (1977)
teaser: It's the only song on Rumours credited to all five band members — pieces of four separate songs were stitched together. The bass riff in the middle is one of rock's most recognizable moments.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the bass line that takes over mid-song — it belonged to a completely different song before the edit.

name: Landslide (1975)
teaser: Stevie Nicks wrote it in Aspen, Colorado, questioning whether she could keep her career going. The song has been covered by everyone from the Smashing Pumpkins to the Dixie Chicks.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the fingerpicked guitar and the quiet key change — it's a song about deciding to go on.

name: Rhiannon (1975)
teaser: Stevie Nicks wrote it about the Welsh witch Rhiannon after reading a novel; the live version turned it into a ritual performance. The band's original was more rock than the hit single.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to Nicks' voice in the final verse — she's singing to the witch, not about her.

name: We Will Rock You (1977)
teaser: The stomp-stomp-clap was recorded by the band stamping and clapping in a studio with no instruments — the entire song is voices, feet and hands. Brian May's guitar solo was added later.

exploreAction.targetName: We Will Rock You (1977) by Queen
exploreAction.instruction: Listen closely — the drum sound is actually people stomping on a wooden floor, not a kit.

name: Don't Stop Me Now (1979)
teaser: Freddie Mercury wrote it at the height of his energy, and the song's '300 degrees' line refers to the temperature of his excitement. It was later voted the happiest song ever by a science study.

exploreAction.targetName: Don't Stop Me Now (1979) by Queen
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the tempo and the piano runs — the song is engineered to feel like it's overheating.

name: Layla (1970)
teaser: Clapton wrote it for Pattie Boyd, George Harrison's wife — and Harrison played on the album anyway. The famous piano coda was written by drummer Jim Gordon, who composed it as a separate piece.

exploreAction.targetName: Layla (1970) by Derek and the Dominos
exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the piano coda after the guitar solo — it's a completely different song that got welded on.

name: Wish You Were Here (1975)
teaser: It was written for Syd Barrett, the band's founder who had left under the strain of fame. The opening sounds like a radio being tuned — the engineer literally recorded someone switching stations.

exploreAction.targetName: Wish You Were Here (1975) by Pink Floyd
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the radio-tuning intro — the song fakes a broken broadcast before the acoustic guitar arrives.

name: Time (1973)
teaser: The song opens with a collage of alarms and ticking clocks recorded at a clock shop. Nick Mason's drum solo in the middle was recorded with a special echo setup.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the clock shop collage — dozens of clocks chiming at once before the band even starts.

name: Money (1973)
teaser: It's in 7/4 time — seven beats per bar instead of the usual four — and the cash-register sound effects were built from a loop of coins and registers. The guitar solo switches to 4/4.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the cash-register loop — and count the beats; the song stumbles in 7/4 on purpose.

name: Paranoid (1970)
teaser: It was written in minutes as a filler track because the band needed a song for the album — the original 'Paranoid' was a different, longer song that didn't work. It became their biggest hit.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to how fast it moves — it was never meant to be the single, just a quick B-side the band knocked out.

name: Iron Man (1970)
teaser: Tony Iommi's riff came first, and Ozzy Osbourne wrote the doom-laden lyrics about a man who sees the apocalypse and is turned to iron. The distorted spoken intro was Ozzy's voice run through a ring modulator.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the opening — Ozzy's voice is processed into something metallic before the riff hits.

name: War Pigs (1970)
teaser: The song's title was changed from 'Walpurgis' to 'War Pigs' — and the anti-war lyric was aimed at the generals who start wars and the politicians who profit. The air-raid siren opens the track.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the siren at the start and the slow, grinding build — it's a warning that takes four minutes to arrive.

name: Smoke on the Water (1972)
teaser: The riff is about a real event: Frank Zappa's concert at the Montreux Casino caught fire, and the band watched the smoke roll over Lake Geneva. The riff has been taught to nearly every guitar player since.

exploreAction.targetName: Smoke on the Water (1972) by Deep Purple
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the famous four-note riff — it was written as the band watched the casino burn across the water.

name: Highway Star (1972)
teaser: It was written on a tour bus in about ten minutes as a joke answer to a journalist's question — 'how do you write songs?' — and the 'highway star' is the car itself.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the organ and guitar trading solos at the end — the song was improvised on a bus ride.

name: Child in Time (1970)
teaser: Ian Gillan's sustained scream near the end is one of the most famous vocal performances in rock — and the song's anti-war theme uses the sound of a scream as its centerpiece.

exploreAction.targetName: Child in Time (1970) by Deep Purple
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to Gillan's scream — it's not a gimmick; the whole song builds toward it.

name: Riders on the Storm (1971)
teaser: It was recorded during an actual thunderstorm, and the rain and thunder in the track are partly real. Jim Morrison whispered his vocal to keep it intimate, and Ray Manzarek played the eerie Fender Rhodes line.

exploreAction.targetName: Riders on the Storm (1971) by The Doors
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the rain — the band recorded the song during a storm and kept the weather in the take.

name: Roadhouse Blues (1970)
teaser: It was cut live in the studio with the band playing together — no overdubs on the rhythm track. Morrison's harmonica and the boogie riff give it a raw, bar-band energy the band rarely captured.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to how loose it sounds compared to the Doors' usual records — this one was recorded live in the room.

name: Knockin' on Heaven's Door (1973)
teaser: It was written for the Sam Peckinpah film Pat Garrett and Billy the Kid, in which Dylan himself acted. The song has been covered by everyone from Eric Clapton to Guns N' Roses.

exploreAction.targetName: Knockin' on Heaven's Door (1973) by Bob Dylan
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the simplicity — two chords and a refrain that turns dying into a lullaby.

name: Wild Horses (1970)
teaser: Keith Richards wrote the melody while struggling with withdrawal, and Gram Parsons — who inspired the country-tinged arrangement — heard it before it was released. The song was recorded with a choir and a pedal steel.

exploreAction.targetName: Wild Horses (1970) by The Rolling Stones
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the pedal steel and the aching last chorus — Richards wrote it in a place he didn't want to be.

name: Brown Sugar (1971)
teaser: It was recorded in Muscle Shoals, Alabama, in one famous session, and the riff-driven song was the Stones' first release on their own label. It topped charts on both sides of the Atlantic.

exploreAction.targetName: Brown Sugar (1971) by The Rolling Stones
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the groove — the band cut it in a single take with the horns and sax recorded live.

name: Angie (1973)
teaser: Keith Richards wrote it with a classical acoustic feel, and the name sparked rumors it was about David Bowie's wife — Richards has always said the title was chosen almost at random. It became their biggest ballad.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the piano and strings arrangement — it's the Stones at their most romantic and most melancholic.

name: Tumbling Dice (1972)
teaser: The song's gambling metaphor came from a Keith Richards rewrite of a country song called 'Good Time Women'. The backing vocals and the loose, boozy groove made it a classic.

exploreAction.targetName: Tumbling Dice (1972) by The Rolling Stones
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to how the band swings — the song is held together by a groove that feels like it could fall apart any second.

name: Starman (1972)
teaser: The song tells of a radio message from an alien, and its appearance on Top of the Pops introduced Ziggy Stardust to Britain. It was written to be the accessible single that opened the album up.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the chorus's wide, soaring melody — it's the moment Ziggy's alien promises to rescue us.

name: Ziggy Stardust (1972)
teaser: The song's narrator is the guitarist in Ziggy's band — a perspective shift that made the album a story told from inside. The guitar riff was Bowie's own, played by Mick Ronson.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the narrative twist — the singer isn't Ziggy; he's the guy in the band watching him fall.

name: Life on Mars? (1971)
teaser: Bowie wrote it as a parody of 'My Way' — the song's narrator is a girl watching a film she doesn't understand, looking for meaning in a world that doesn't explain itself. The piano and strings make it feel cinematic.

exploreAction.targetName: Life on Mars? (1971) by David Bowie
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the chord changes — they keep rising like a film score, while the lyrics ask questions that never get answers.

name: Heroes (1977)
teaser: Recorded at Hansa Studio right by the Berlin Wall, Bowie sang farther from the microphone as the take went on so the louder moments would push the sound to its edge. The song is about two lovers meeting at the wall.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to how his voice strains and distorts toward the end — he deliberately out-sang the microphone's limits.

name: Waterloo (1974)
teaser: ABBA won the 1974 Eurovision Song Contest with it, launching their global career. The song is a metaphor of surrender — 'my Waterloo' — set to a glam-influenced pop stomp.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the chorus's surrender — a love confession dressed as a military defeat.

name: Mamma Mia (1975)
teaser: The song's nonsense-title chorus was the band's joke about Italian restaurant menus — 'mamma mia' stuck anyway. It later inspired the stage musical and film of the same name.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the sigh in the chorus — the song is about relapsing into a love you know is bad for you.

name: SOS (1975)
teaser: Written during the band's own marital troubles, the song's 'SOS' chorus is a genuine cry for help wrapped in a pop melody. It became ABBA's first big international hit after Eurovision.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the contrast — a desperate lyric sung over the brightest, catchiest pop melody.

name: Fernando (1976)
teaser: It was originally written in Swedish about two old revolutionaries remembering a war — the English version kept the setting vague enough to become a global ballad. It's one of their biggest-selling singles worldwide.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the storytelling — two old men reminiscing about a battle, sung as a gentle ballad.

name: Let's Stay Together (1972)
teaser: The opening drum roll and the warm horn riff make it one of the most beloved soul records ever. Green sang it in one take with the band live in the studio.

exploreAction.targetName: Let's Stay Together (1972) by Al Green
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the first two bars — the drum roll sets up a song that never loses its patience.

name: Let's Get It On (1973)
teaser: Gaye wrote it as a sensual slow jam, but the original demo had gospel lyrics. The song's groove was built around the bass and Gaye's half-sung, half-spoken delivery.

exploreAction.targetName: Let's Get It On (1973) by Marvin Gaye
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to how Gaye talks and sings at the same time — the vocals ride the groove like a conversation.

name: What's Going On (1971)
teaser: The song started when Four Tops member Obie Benson saw police beating protesters and co-wrote it with Gaye and Al Cleveland. Gaye layered his own vocals three times to create a chorus of one.

exploreAction.targetName: What's Going On (1971) by Marvin Gaye
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the stacked vocals — Gaye sings every part himself, making a one-man crowd.

name: Mercy Mercy Me (The Ecology) (1971)
teaser: It was one of the first mainstream pop songs about environmental destruction — 'oil wasted on the ocean and upon our seas'. The album's soft, jazzy arrangements made the message float instead of shout.

exploreAction.targetName: Mercy Mercy Me (The Ecology) (1971) by Marvin Gaye
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the gentle, almost resigned delivery — the song mourns instead of marches.

name: Superfly (1972)
teaser: The title track of the Blaxploitation film Super Fly used wah-wah guitar and a funky bassline to tell the story of a cocaine dealer trying to get out. Mayfield wrote and arranged the entire soundtrack.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the wah-wah guitar — it's the sound of the film's neon, and the cautionary tale underneath the funk.

name: Get Up (I Feel Like Being a) Sex Machine (1970)
teaser: The track's stuttering guitar and Brown's shouts built the template for funk — drummers still quote its break. Brown's 'get up' chant was improvised in the studio.

exploreAction.targetName: Get Up (I Feel Like Being a) Sex Machine (1970) by James Brown
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the drum break and the guitar chokes — this is the blueprint nearly every funk and hip-hop break came from.

name: Living for the City (1973)
teaser: The song's middle section is a mini radio play: a young man from the South arrives in New York and gets arrested for a crime he didn't commit, complete with city street sounds Wonder recorded himself.

exploreAction.targetName: Living for the City (1973) by Stevie Wonder
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the street-noise skit in the middle — footsteps, traffic, an arrest — the song becomes a short film.

name: Signed, Sealed, Delivered I'm Yours (1970)
teaser: Wonder wrote it on the spot when a studio session ran long, and the horn line and his soaring 'ooh baby' made it an instant classic. It was later used as a campaign song for Barack Obama.

exploreAction.targetName: Signed, Sealed, Delivered I'm Yours (1970) by Stevie Wonder
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the horn intro and the way Wonder's voice leaps on the final hook — pure joy.

name: Sir Duke (1976)
teaser: It's a tribute to Duke Ellington and the musicians who inspired Wonder. The horn section was arranged to sound like a full band, and the song topped the charts a decade after Ellington's death.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the horn riffs trading with the bass — the whole song is one long thank-you note to jazz.

name: September (1978)
teaser: The 'ba-dee-ya' hook was originally a placeholder — the band never wrote real words for it, and the scat became the most memorable part. The '21st night of September' date is just a date that sounded good.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the 'ba-dee-ya' — it was a placeholder syllable that became the song's identity.

name: Le Freak (1978)
teaser: Nile Rodgers and Bernard Edwards wrote it after being denied entry to Studio 54 — the original chorus was 'Aaaaah, fuck off!', which became 'freak out'. It's one of the best-selling singles of all time.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the 'freak out' chant — it started as an angry insult to a nightclub doorman.

name: Good Times (1979)
teaser: The bass line is the most sampled in music history — it's the backbone of 'Rapper's Delight' and countless hip-hop records. Nile Rodgers wrote the riff after his guitar was stolen and he replaced it with a new sound.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the bass line — it's been recycled into dozens of hip-hop classics; hear the original here.

name: Staying Alive (1977)
teaser: The bass line was an afterthought, but it became the song's pulse — and the song's rhythm famously matches the tempo used for CPR chest compressions. The brothers recorded the vocals with their signature falsetto.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the bass line keeping perfect time — it's so steady it's used to time CPR compressions.

name: Night Fever (1977)
teaser: Written for Saturday Night Fever, it was the last song recorded for the album and became the defining disco track of the era. The song's title came from the film's working title.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the falsetto and the driving beat — the song was written in one night and became an era.

name: YMCA (1978)
teaser: Written for the Village People — a group of costume-clad archetypes — the song's YMCA hand-dance became a worldwide phenomenon. The group themselves were surprised it became a wedding and sports staple.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the call-and-response chorus — the song is a letter to a community center, not a place.

name: Love Train (1972)
teaser: The Gamble & Huff production made it an anthem of unity — 'people all over the world, join hands'. It was one of the first soul songs with an explicitly global message.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the train-whistle horns and the rolling rhythm — the song is a ticket to nowhere and everywhere.

name: Midnight Train to Georgia (1973)
teaser: It was originally written as 'Midnight Plane to Houston' — the writers changed plane to train for a warmer, more soulful image. The Pips' backing vocals made it one of the great soul records of the decade.

exploreAction.targetName: Midnight Train to Georgia (1973) by Gladys Knight & the Pips
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the Pips answering Gladys line by line — the song is a duet between her lead and their echoes.

name: Killing Me Softly with His Song (1973)
teaser: The song was inspired by Don McLean's live performance of 'American Pie' — writer Lori Lieberman was moved to tears at a show. Flack's version won Record of the Year at the Grammys.

exploreAction.targetName: Killing Me Softly with His Song (1973) by Roberta Flack
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to how softly the verses begin — the song creeps up on you exactly like the story it tells.

name: Walk on the Wild Side (1972)
teaser: The bass line is played by Herbie Flowers on a double bass recorded twice — an octave apart — creating its distinctive slide. The song's characters were real people from Andy Warhol's Factory scene.

exploreAction.targetName: Walk on the Wild Side (1972) by Lou Reed
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the bass — it's one player doubling himself, and the sliding notes are the whole groove.

name: Perfect Day (1972)
teaser: Written while Reed was working as a typist at his father's firm, the song's calm surface hides a much darker undercurrent. The BBC later made a charity cover featuring dozens of stars.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the sweet, simple melody — and notice how the chorus swells with strings just once before pulling back.

name: Marquee Moon (1977)
teaser: The ten-minute centerpiece of the band's debut is built on two guitars interlocking in a marathon of solos — Richard Lloyd and Tom Verlaine never once play the same line. It defined New York punk's artier side.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the two guitars trading at the end — they play separate, interlocking solos that never resolve together.

name: Psycho Killer (1977)
teaser: David Byrne wrote the French verses because he was self-conscious about his voice — the 'qu'est-ce que c'est' chorus became iconic anyway. Tina Weymouth's bassline drives the whole nervous groove.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the bassline — it's the heartbeat of the paranoia, ticking under every verse.

name: Roxanne (1978)
teaser: Sting wrote it after seeing prostitutes in Paris — the 'red light' of the lyric is literal. The song's reggae-influenced beat was the band's signature move.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the way the reggae beat turns into a rock drive on the chorus — the tension is the whole song.

name: Message in a Bottle (1979)
teaser: Sting wrote the riff while trying to copy a reggae pattern on guitar, and the lyric about isolation became a global hit. It was the band's first UK No. 1.

exploreAction.targetName: Message in a Bottle (1979) by The Police
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the guitar riff — it was an accident that became one of the most copied riffs in new wave.

name: God Save the Queen (1977)
teaser: Released during Queen Elizabeth II's Silver Jubilee, the song was banned by the BBC and topped the charts anyway. Its 'no future' chorus captured the mood of a generation.

exploreAction.targetName: God Save the Queen (1977) by Sex Pistols
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the sneer in 'no future' — the song was banned from radio and sold hundreds of thousands anyway.

name: Anarchy in the U.K. (1976)
teaser: The song's 'I am an antichrist' opening was pure provocation, and its release helped trigger the punk explosion in Britain. It was recorded in one take with the band playing live.

exploreAction.targetName: Anarchy in the U.K. (1976) by Sex Pistols
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to how fast it ends — barely three minutes, and the band is already gone.

name: Blitzkrieg Bop (1976)
teaser: The 'Hey ho, let's go' chant made it the anthem of punk's first wave. It was written by Tommy Ramone, the drummer, who was the band's most experienced musician.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the count-in — one, two, three, four, and the whole world speeds up.

name: Sheena Is a Punk Rocker (1977)
teaser: The song's celebration of a California punk girl helped define the scene's outsider mythology. It was recorded in a single day with the band playing live in the studio.

exploreAction.targetName: Sheena Is a Punk Rocker (1977) by Ramones
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the surf-guitar lick under the punk energy — the Ramones were a beach band that sped up.

name: Search and Destroy (1973)
teaser: Iggy Pop's primal howl and James Williamson's razor riff made it the blueprint for punk aggression — David Bowie produced the album. The lyric 'I'm a streetwalking cheetah with a heart full of napalm' became legendary.

exploreAction.targetName: Search and Destroy (1973) by The Stooges
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the riff's raw, untuned power — the album was mixed fast to capture the band's live noise.

name: Maggie May (1971)
teaser: The mandolin intro was added as an afterthought, and the song about a young man and an older woman topped the charts in the US and UK simultaneously. Stewart wrote it about his own teenage experience.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the mandolin — it was an accident that became the song's signature sound.

name: You're So Vain (1972)
teaser: The subject of the song has been a mystery for decades — everyone from Warren Beatty to Mick Jagger has been named (Jagger sings backing vocals). Simon has only ever hinted at the answer.

exploreAction.targetName: You're So Vain (1972) by Carly Simon
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to Jagger's backing vocals in the chorus — he's singing on a song people think is about him.

name: Piano Man (1973)
teaser: Joel wrote it about his real life playing piano in a Los Angeles bar, and the characters — 'Paul is a real estate novelist' — were regulars. The harmonica and accordion give it its barroom feel.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the accordion and harmonica — Joel recorded them in a studio bar set to feel like the lounge he actually played.

name: New York State of Mind (1976)
teaser: Joel wrote it on the drive home after years in California, capturing the feeling of coming back to the city. The sax solo by Richie Cannata became one of the song's signatures.

exploreAction.targetName: New York State of Mind (1976) by Billy Joel
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the sax solo — it's the sound of the skyline appearing over the bridge.

name: Band on the Run (1973)
teaser: The song's three-part structure tells of prisoners escaping — the band recorded it at EMI's Nigeria studio during a turbulent trip where their demo tapes were stolen. The medley became a Grammy winner.

exploreAction.targetName: Band on the Run (1973) by Paul McCartney & Wings
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to how the song changes gears three times — escape, a night on the run, and a sunrise resolution.

name: Maybe I'm Amazed (1970)
teaser: Written in the aftermath of the Beatles' breakup, it's McCartney's most personal song — an ode to Linda for holding him together. It was recorded with just Paul on all instruments.

exploreAction.targetName: Maybe I'm Amazed (1970) by Paul McCartney
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the one-man band — McCartney played every instrument, recorded in his home studio.

name: My Sweet Lord (1970)
