teaser: It was the first solo No. 1 by a Beatle — and it later lost a plagiarism suit over its similarity to the Chiffons' 'He's So Fine'. Harrison said the similarity was unconscious.

exploreAction.targetName: My Sweet Lord (1970) by George Harrison
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the gospel chorus building the 'Hallelujah' into a devotional wall of voices.

name: Candle in the Wind (1973)
teaser: Bernie Taupin wrote the lyric about Marilyn Monroe — 'a candle in the wind' — and the song became famous again in 1997 when Elton rewrote it for Princess Diana's funeral.

exploreAction.targetName: Candle in the Wind (1973) by Elton John
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the piano arpeggios — the song is a eulogy that outlived its subject twice.

name: Tiny Dancer (1971)
teaser: Bernie Taupin wrote it about his then-wife, a seamstress's assistant — the 'tiny dancer' with 'blue jean baby' eyes. The song became famous again decades later thanks to the film Almost Famous.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the middle section where the song nearly stops — then the piano brings it back for the final chorus.

name: Your Song (1970)
teaser: Bernie Taupin wrote the lyrics at age 17 in about twenty minutes, and Elton set them to music the same day. The opening piano notes are the sound of a songwriter working it out in real time.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the opening — the piano stumbles before the song begins, and they kept that first take.

name: Goodbye Yellow Brick Road (1973)
teaser: The title track of the album uses L. Frank Baum's Oz imagery to tell a story of rejecting fame and going home. The song's waltz-like verses lead to one of Elton's grandest choruses.

exploreAction.targetName: Goodbye Yellow Brick Road (1973) by Elton John
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the shift from verse to chorus — the song literally climbs out of the yellow brick road.

name: Bennie and the Jets (1973)
teaser: The fake live crowd noise was added to make it sound like a concert bootleg, and the song's stuttering beat became one of Elton's biggest hits. Radio stations played it despite the fake applause.

exploreAction.targetName: Bennie and the Jets (1973) by Elton John
exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the crowd noise — the band faked a live recording to make the song feel like a bootleg.

name: Me and Bobby McGee (1971)
teaser: Kris Kristofferson wrote it, and Joplin's version became her only No. 1 — released just after her death. The 'freedom's just another word for nothing left to lose' line is one of the most quoted in songwriting.

exploreAction.targetName: Me and Bobby McGee (1971) by Janis Joplin
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the freedom line — Joplin's voice turns a goodbye into a celebration.

name: Have You Ever Seen the Rain? (1971)
teaser: John Fogerty wrote it about the band's own breakup — the rain falling while the sun shines. It was one of the last CCR singles before the group dissolved.

exploreAction.targetName: Have You Ever Seen the Rain? (1971) by Creedence Clearwater Revival
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the paradox in the title — the song is about smiling through the end of a band.

name: A Horse with No Name (1972)
teaser: The band wrote it about the desert crossing in the film Easy Rider — and critics accused it of sounding like Neil Young, which the band took as a compliment. It became their only No. 1.

exploreAction.targetName: A Horse with No Name (1972) by America
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the sparse, wandering groove — the song is a road trip with no destination.

name: The Joker (1973)
teaser: The lyric 'the pompatus of love' is a word Steve Miller made up — it has spawned decades of debate about what it means. The song is built around a bass line and a whistle.

exploreAction.targetName: The Joker (1973) by Steve Miller Band
exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the whistle — and try to figure out what 'pompatus' means; nobody has ever agreed.

name: Fly Like an Eagle (1976)
teaser: The spacey, slowed-down intro was created by recording at half speed and playing the tape back faster — giving the 'eagle' its dreamy glide. The song's cosmic soul made it an instant classic.

exploreAction.targetName: Fly Like an Eagle (1976) by Steve Miller Band
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the intro's wobbling, slowed-down sound — the tape trick makes it feel like it's from space.

name: More Than a Feeling (1976)
teaser: Tom Scholz recorded the demos in his basement on a homemade tape setup, and the label signed the band based on those bedroom tapes. The song's guitar intro became one of rock's most famous.

exploreAction.targetName: More Than a Feeling (1976) by Boston
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the guitar intro — it was recorded in a basement on a prototype of a guitar pedal Scholz built himself.

name: Carry on Wayward Son (1976)
teaser: The song's a cappella intro and changing time signatures made it a prog-rock radio staple. Its theme of a wanderer finding purpose made it an instant arena anthem.

exploreAction.targetName: Carry on Wayward Son (1976) by Kansas
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the intro's layered vocals — the band arranged themselves like a choir before the guitars hit.

name: Dust in the Wind (1977)
teaser: Guitarist Kerry Livgren was practicing a fingerpicking exercise when his wife suggested he write lyrics to it — the result was one of the most famous acoustic songs in rock. The words came from Ecclesiastes.

exploreAction.targetName: Dust in the Wind (1977) by Kansas
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the fingerpicking pattern — it was a guitar warm-up exercise before it was a song.

name: Barracuda (1977)
teaser: Ann Wilson wrote the lyric in fury after a record company tried to brand the band with a fabricated backstory. The riff-driven song became their defiant signature.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the anger in Ann Wilson's voice — the song is a letter telling the label to back off.

name: Crazy on You (1976)
teaser: The song opens with a flamenco-style acoustic guitar that suddenly slams into a hard rock riff — Nancy Wilson's acoustic intro was a tribute to classical guitarists. The contrast made it a classic.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the flamenco intro — it's a Spanish guitar piece that turns into a rock song mid-bar.

name: Take It Easy (1972)
teaser: Jackson Browne co-wrote it — the Eagles finished his unfinished song and it became their first single. The famous line 'standing on a corner in Winslow, Arizona' is a real place with a real corner.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the easy, rolling rhythm — the song's whole philosophy is in its title.

name: Desperado (1973)
teaser: The band's outlaw-themed ballad was written by Glenn Frey and Don Henley about a gunslinger who won't let anyone in. It's been covered by dozens of artists, from Linda Ronstadt to Johnny Cash.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the piano and the final 'you better let somebody love you' — the song is a plea to the loner.

name: Lyin' Eyes (1975)
teaser: The song tells of a woman cheating on an older husband, and its country-rock sway won the band a Grammy. The famous story in the lyric — the downtown bar — was based on a real LA scene.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the story in the verses — each one advances the same unhappy marriage.

name: New Kid in Town (1976)
teaser: The song's theme — that someone newer always comes along — was written while the band watched the music scene churn around them. It was their first of five consecutive No. 1 hits.

exploreAction.targetName: New Kid in Town (1976) by Eagles
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the harmony vocals — the Eagles' layered voices are the whole hook here.

name: Life in the Fast Lane (1976)
teaser: Joe Walsh's driving riff came from a jam session, and Glenn Frey wrote the lyric about the LA lifestyle of too much money and too little time. The song captures the album's dark undercurrent.

exploreAction.targetName: Life in the Fast Lane (1976) by Eagles
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the riff — it was a leftover jam that Walsh brought to the band and they never let go.

name: Take Me Home, Country Roads (1971)
teaser: It was written by Bill Danoff and Taffy Nivert — Denver contributed the final melody — and the song made West Virginia famous despite none of the writers ever living there. It became the state's anthem.

exploreAction.targetName: Take Me Home, Country Roads (1971) by John Denver
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the chorus's longing — the song made strangers homesick for a place they'd never been.

name: Rocky Mountain High (1972)
teaser: Denver wrote it about his love of Colorado, and the song's nature imagery helped launch the environmental movement's soundtrack. It became Colorado's state song.

exploreAction.targetName: Rocky Mountain High (1972) by John Denver
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the acoustic guitar and the mountains in the melody — Denver wrote it after moving to Aspen.

name: Annie's Song (1974)
teaser: Denver wrote it in about ten minutes on a ski lift, inspired by his wife Annie — 'you fill up my senses'. It became one of the best-selling love songs of the decade.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the flute and the swelling strings — the song is a catalog of everything one person is to another.

name: Margaritaville (1977)
teaser: The song invented a state of mind — the name 'Margaritaville' is a real, fictional place where the worries wash away with the tide. It made Buffett a star and created an entire lifestyle brand.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the steel drum and the lazy rhythm — the song is a permanent vacation with a hangover.

name: Livin' on a Prayer (1986)
teaser: Richie Sambora's talk box — the guitar that sounds like it's talking — made the 'whoa, we're halfway there' chorus iconic. It was almost cut from the album until Sambora convinced Jon Bon Jovi to keep it.

exploreAction.targetName: Livin' on a Prayer (1986) by Bon Jovi
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the talk-box guitar in the chorus — the guitar is literally singing the words.

name: You Give Love a Bad Name (1986)
teaser: The song's chorus was originally written for another artist entirely — the band repurposed the hook and it became their first No. 1. The opening power chord is one of the most recognizable in rock.

exploreAction.targetName: You Give Love a Bad Name (1986) by Bon Jovi
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the opening chord and the machine-gun chorus — a song built from one unstoppable hook.

name: Jump (1984)
teaser: The song is built around a synth riff — not guitar — which was a shock from the band that made guitar solos famous. David Lee Roth wrote the 'might as well jump' lyric after seeing a news report of a suicide attempt.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the keyboard riff that carries the whole song — no guitar lead until the final solo.

name: Panama (1984)
teaser: The song is a tribute to a car — Eddie Van Halen recorded the sound of his own engine revving for the intro. The title track's riff has become one of rock's endurance tests.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the engine rev at the start — that's Eddie Van Halen's actual car.

name: Run to the Hills (1982)
teaser: The galloping bassline and Steve Harris's history-inspired lyric tell of the colonization of the Americas from both sides — the natives' and the settlers'. It became the band's first UK hit.

exploreAction.targetName: Run to the Hills (1982) by Iron Maiden
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the galloping bass — the song rides like a cavalry charge across its own history lesson.

name: The Number of the Beast (1982)
teaser: The spoken intro was recorded by horror actor Vincent Price, and the song's title caused protests from religious groups who thought the band were literal devil worshippers. It became a metal milestone.

exploreAction.targetName: The Number of the Beast (1982) by Iron Maiden
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to Vincent Price's voice at the start — the actor agreed to narrate in one session.

name: Master of Puppets (1986)
teaser: The title track is an anti-addiction song — the 'master' is the drug — and its centerpiece is a long instrumental section with a clean-guitar interlude that was unprecedented for thrash. It's one of the most important metal songs ever written.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the clean-guitar break in the middle — the song lets go completely before the riff returns.

name: One (1988)
teaser: It's based on the anti-war novel Johnny Got His Gun, about a soldier who loses all his senses — the machine-gun drums at the end are the song's climax. The band later made a music video using the film's footage.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to how the song builds from quiet single notes to full machine-gun chaos — it's a descent, not a chorus.

name: Back in Black (1980)
teaser: It was written as a tribute to Bon Scott, who died just months before — the title is the band's way of saying they were moving on. The album has sold over 50 million copies.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the opening riff — it was written the day the band decided to carry on after Bon Scott's death.

name: You Shook Me All Night Long (1980)
teaser: It was the first AC/DC song with Brian Johnson to be written, and its instantly recognizable riff made it a wedding and stadium staple for decades. It's one of the best-selling rock singles ever.

exploreAction.targetName: You Shook Me All Night Long (1980) by AC/DC
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the riff — simple enough to whistle, heavy enough to fill a stadium.

name: Crazy Train (1980)
teaser: It launched Ozzy's solo career after his Black Sabbath departure, and Randy Rhoads' riff became one of the most famous in metal history. The 'I'm going off the rails' scream is pure Ozzy.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the opening riff — Randy Rhoads wrote it as a classical exercise before it became metal's most copied intro.

name: Mr. Crowley (1980)
teaser: The song is about the occultist Aleister Crowley, whose teachings fascinated the young Ozzy. The keyboard line and Rhoads' solo give it a gothic, theatrical air.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the church-like organ and the solo — the song is a haunted house in four minutes.

name: Holy Diver (1983)
teaser: Ronnie James Dio wrote the song about a diver descending into the sea of faith, and its slow-burning opening riff became one of metal's most iconic. The video, with Dio in knight armor, is legendary.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the opening riff's long, patient build — the song takes its time before it lets loose.

name: Rainbow in the Dark (1983)
teaser: The song's famous keyboard riff was written by Dio's bandmate as a joke demo — Dio added the lyric about searching for a rainbow in the dark. It became his signature.

exploreAction.targetName: Rainbow in the Dark (1983) by Dio
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the keyboard riff — it was a throwaway demo the band almost didn't use.

name: Pour Some Sugar on Me (1987)
teaser: The band built the song on a drum machine and a chant, and it was written late at night during the Hysteria sessions in Dublin. It became their biggest American hit.

exploreAction.targetName: Pour Some Sugar on Me (1987) by Def Leppard
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the percussion-driven intro — the song started as a drum machine loop and a chant.

name: Photograph (1983)
teaser: The song's video — a day in the life of a rock band — helped make MTV. The lyric was written about a girl in a photograph, and the riff became the band's calling card.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the riff that opens the song — it was written the morning of the session, in minutes.

name: Kickstart My Heart (1989)
teaser: Nikki Sixx wrote it about his near-fatal overdose and the adrenaline of being revived — the 'kickstart my heart' is literal. The song became the band's biggest hit.

exploreAction.targetName: Kickstart My Heart (1989) by Mötley Crüe
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the racing riff — it's a heart restarting, written by the man who flatlined.

name: Welcome to the Jungle (1987)
teaser: Axl Rose wrote the lyrics about arriving in LA with nothing — the 'jungle' is the city. The band recorded the demo in one night and it became the opening statement of Appetite for Destruction.

exploreAction.targetName: Welcome to the Jungle (1987) by Guns N' Roses
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the opening — the song starts with a warning before the riff even arrives.

name: Paradise City (1987)
teaser: The chorus was written years before the verses — Axl Rose had the 'take me down to paradise city' hook since his teenage band days. The outro solo section became one of rock's great endings.

exploreAction.targetName: Paradise City (1987) by Guns N' Roses
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the last two minutes — the song builds into a triple-guitar outro that never wants to stop.

name: Every Rose Has Its Thorn (1988)
teaser: Bret Michaels wrote it in a hotel room after a phone breakup — the line 'every rose has its thorn' came from seeing a rose on a payphone. It became the band's only No. 1.

exploreAction.targetName: Every Rose Has Its Thorn (1988) by Poison
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the acoustic intro — the whole song came from one sad phone call and a rose on a payphone.

name: Fight for Your Right (1986)
teaser: It was written as a parody of party songs — the band was surprised when people took it literally and made it an anthem. The party-crash video became an MTV staple.

exploreAction.targetName: Fight for Your Right (1986) by Beastie Boys
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the sarcasm in the verses — the song was mocking the party records it now defines.

name: No Sleep Till Brooklyn (1986)
teaser: The guitar solo is played by Kerry King of Slayer — the band hired a thrash metal guitarist to make the song sound more rock. It's one of the first rap-rock crossovers.

exploreAction.targetName: No Sleep Till Brooklyn (1986) by Beastie Boys
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the guitar solo — that's the Slayer guitarist shredding on a rap song.

name: The Message (1982)
teaser: It was the first mainstream hip-hop record about social issues — 'don't push me 'cause I'm close to the edge'. The beat's tension was built from a synthesizer line that still gets sampled today.
byline: Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five

exploreAction.targetName: The Message (1982) by Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the synthesized tension loop — it's the sound of the city the lyrics describe.

name: Rapper's Delight (1979)
teaser: It was the first hip-hop single to become a national hit — a 15-minute rap over a borrowed bassline. The band that wrote the backing track sued for credit and eventually got it.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the bassline — it was taken from a disco hit, and the lawsuit over it changed how hip-hop credited samples.

name: Planet Rock (1982)
teaser: It built hip-hop's electronic sound by sampling Kraftwerk's 'Trans-Europe Express' — one of the first records to treat another band's music as raw material. It created electro.

exploreAction.targetName: Planet Rock (1982) by Afrika Bambaataa & the Soulsonic Force
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the Kraftwerk synth lines underneath — this is where electronic dance music and hip-hop first met.

name: Rockit (1983)
teaser: The robotic, scratching soundscape won the first MTV Video Music Award for a video with no humans in it — just mechanical puppets. It introduced scratching to a mainstream audience.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the turntable scratching — a jazz legend brought DJ culture to the pop charts.

name: Straight Outta Compton (1988)
teaser: The title track introduced the world to gangsta rap — a raw, unflinching portrait of Compton. Its opening line became one of the most quoted in hip-hop history.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the aggression in the delivery — the song is a declaration of a place and a stance.

name: Fight the Power (1989)
teaser: Written for Spike Lee's Do the Right Thing, the song's wall of sirens and Chuck D's booming delivery made it a political rallying cry. It's been called one of the most important protest songs ever.

exploreAction.targetName: Fight the Power (1989) by Public Enemy
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the siren samples and the sheer volume of the production — the song is built to be played loud in public.

name: It Takes Two (1988)
teaser: The track's famous horn and drum sample from a James Brown record became the most reused loop in hip-hop history. It took the genre's party side to the mainstream.
byline: Rob Base and DJ E-Z Rock

exploreAction.targetName: It Takes Two (1988) by Rob Base and DJ E-Z Rock
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the horn loop — it's lifted from a James Brown song and became hip-hop's most-copied break.

name: Push It (1987)
teaser: The duo's label pressed them to record a dance track, and 'Push It' — originally a B-side — became one of the biggest rap records by a female group. It broke ground for women in hip-hop.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the simple synth pulse — a B-side that became a movement.

name: Walk This Way (1986)
teaser: The collaboration between a rap group and a rock band revived both careers and introduced hip-hop to MTV's rock audience. The video's wall-breaking scene is legendary.

exploreAction.targetName: Walk This Way (1986) by Run-DMC feat. Aerosmith
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the handoff — the rap verses and the rock chorus trade off like a conversation between genres.

name: Like a Prayer (1989)
teaser: The gospel choir and religious imagery caused a worldwide backlash, but the song became one of her defining records. The video was condemned by the Vatican and praised by critics.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the gospel choir entering — the song builds from a confession into a full church service.

name: Like a Virgin (1984)
teaser: The wedding bells intro and the suggestive chorus made it her first No. 1 — and the title was written by two men who didn't know Madonna. The song has outlived every controversy around it.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the wedding bells at the start — the song opens like a ceremony and turns into a dance floor.

name: Material Girl (1984)
teaser: The video recreated Marilyn Monroe's 'Diamonds Are a Girl's Best Friend' number, and the song's chorus became shorthand for 80s excess. Madonna later said she regretted the message.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the chorus — it's a critique of materialism sung so catchy nobody heard the irony.

name: Into the Groove (1985)
teaser: It was written for the film Desperately Seeking Susan, in which Madonna starred — and it's often called the song that defined mid-80s dance pop. It was never released as a US single, yet became one of her most played.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the layered synths and the spoken intro — a film soundtrack that became a club classic.

name: Express Yourself (1989)
teaser: The feminist anthem told women not to settle for a man who doesn't appreciate them. The video, directed by David Fincher, referenced Fritz Lang's Metropolis.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the driving beat and the message — the song demands equality on the dance floor.

name: Girls Just Want to Have Fun (1983)
teaser: It was written by Robert Hazard as a man's song about a wild girl — Lauper flipped the perspective and turned it into an anthem of female freedom. The video is one of MTV's most beloved.

exploreAction.targetName: Girls Just Want to Have Fun (1983) by Cyndi Lauper
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the chorus's celebration — the song was rewritten from a man's joke into a woman's declaration.

name: Time After Time (1983)
teaser: Lauper co-wrote it with Rob Hyman, and the song's promise — 'if you're lost you can look and you will find me' — made it one of the most covered ballads of the decade. It was written in one session.

exploreAction.targetName: Time After Time (1983) by Cyndi Lauper
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the tenderness in the chorus — the song was written in a single afternoon.

name: True Colors (1986)
teaser: The title track's message of self-acceptance made it an anthem for the LGBTQ community, and Lauper later co-founded a charity named after the song. It's one of the most sincere pop records of the decade.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the simplicity — just piano, voice and a promise that your true colors are beautiful.

name: Total Eclipse of the Heart (1983)
teaser: Jim Steinman wrote it as a gothic power ballad, and the song's operatic scale made it a worldwide No. 1. It holds a record for its length and drama among 80s hits.

exploreAction.targetName: Total Eclipse of the Heart (1983) by Bonnie Tyler
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the key changes and the choir — Jim Steinman wrote it as a love story with the volume turned to eleven.

name: Holding Out for a Hero (1984)
teaser: Jim Steinman wrote it for the film Footloose, and its soaring chorus has been used in countless movies and shows since. The song's martial drums make it feel like a quest.

exploreAction.targetName: Holding Out for a Hero (1984) by Bonnie Tyler
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the drum march and the key change — the song is a job posting for a savior.

name: Footloose (1984)
teaser: The title track of the film — Loggins was asked to write a song about a town where dancing is banned, and the result topped charts worldwide. It's one of the defining soundtracks of the decade.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the guitar riff that opens the song — it's a dance floor emergency in four notes.

name: Danger Zone (1986)
teaser: Written for Top Gun, the song's title came from a phrase in the film's script. Loggins' roaring vocal made it the sound of 80s blockbuster cinema.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the synth-driven engine — the song is a jet taking off with a vocal attached.

name: Everybody Wants to Rule the World (1985)
teaser: The song was written as a commentary on the Cold War's power games — and its warm, hypnotic chorus became one of the decade's defining sounds. It was their first US No. 1.

exploreAction.targetName: Everybody Wants to Rule the World (1985) by Tears for Fears
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the rolling synth bass and the weary chorus — a warning wrapped in a lullaby.

name: Shout (1985)
teaser: The song's message is about the cycle of abuse — 'shout, shout, let it all out' — and its slow-burning build became an anthem. The extended version is a masterpiece of 80s production.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to how slowly the song builds — the chorus takes nearly two minutes to arrive.

name: Mad World (1982)
teaser: The original was a synth-pop single — it became a global hit again decades later when Gary Jules covered it in a stripped-down piano version for the film Donnie Darko.

exploreAction.targetName: Mad World (1982) by Tears for Fears
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the original's bright synths — it sounds nothing like the sad piano version everyone remembers.

name: Don't You (Forget About Me) (1985)
teaser: Written for The Breakfast Club, the band recorded it almost as an afterthought — the song's 'la la la' ending became one of cinema's most famous. It was Simple Minds' only US No. 1.

exploreAction.targetName: Don't You (Forget About Me) (1985) by Simple Minds
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the famous 'la la la' outro — the band almost turned the song down before recording it.

name: The Power of Love (1985)
teaser: Written for Back to the Future, the song's joyful brass and chorus became inseparable from the film. Lewis also appeared in the movie as a judge.

exploreAction.targetName: The Power of Love (1985) by Huey Lewis and the News
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the horns — the song is pure 1985, built to accompany a time machine.

name: Careless Whisper (1984)
teaser: George Michael wrote it at 17, and the saxophone riff — played by a session musician — became one of the most famous in pop history. The song's guilt-filled lyric is about cheating.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the sax intro — it was written when Michael was still a teenager.

name: Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go (1984)
teaser: The song's title came from a note Andrew Ridgeley left for George Michael — 'wake me up before you go-go'. The upbeat, day-glo pop became the sound of 1984.

exploreAction.targetName: Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go (1984) by Wham!
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the hand-claps and the sheer cheerfulness — a note left on a fridge became a global hit.

name: Faith (1987)
teaser: The song opens with a jukebox and a spoken 'well, I guess it would be nice', and its rockabilly beat and guitar riff made it a solo statement. The video, with the leather jacket and guitar, defined his look.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the intro's record-scratch and jukebox — the song announces itself like a jukebox coming alive.

name: Karma Chameleon (1983)
teaser: Boy George wrote the chorus about the fear of being yourself — 'you come and go' — and the song's country-blues stomp made it an international No. 1. It was the decade's biggest-selling UK single.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the stomp and the harmonica — a song about identity disguised as a dance hit.

name: Tainted Love (1981)
teaser: It's a cover of a 1965 northern soul record by Gloria Jones — the synth version became the biggest-selling single in the UK in 1981. The beat was built on a drum machine riff.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the relentless drum machine pulse — the song never drops it, even through the breakdown.

name: Don't You Want Me (1981)
teaser: The song's lyric is a fight between two lovers — and the video, set on a film studio lot, made the band stars. It became one of the defining records of synth-pop.

exploreAction.targetName: Don't You Want Me (1981) by The Human League
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the two singers trading accusations — the song is an argument set to a dance beat.

name: Blue Monday (1983)
teaser: It's the best-selling 12-inch single of all time, and the band famously lost money on it because the sleeve design cost more than the profit per copy. The bassline and the drum machine pattern are legendary.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the drum machine intro — it's been sampled and copied more times than almost any other beat.

name: Bizarre Love Triangle (1986)
teaser: The song's title describes its own lyrics — a love triangle told from the middle. The layered synth arpeggios became the template for electronic pop.

exploreAction.targetName: Bizarre Love Triangle (1986) by New Order
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the arpeggio sequence — it was built on a cheap synth and became dance music's blueprint.

name: True Faith (1987)
teaser: The song's euphoric chorus is undercut by lyrics about escaping the past — 'I used to think that the day would never come'. The video, with the dancing masks, won awards.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the contrast — a joyful melody singing about the pain of growing up.

name: Just Can't Get Enough (1981)
teaser: It was written by Vince Clarke, who left the band right after — the song's joyful synth-pop is a farewell to the band's early sound. It's one of the most beloved songs of the decade.

exploreAction.targetName: Just Can't Get Enough (1981) by Depeche Mode
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the bouncy synth riff — the writer quit the band immediately after recording it.

name: Personal Jesus (1989)
teaser: The driving guitar riff was a radical turn for the synth band — the song was inspired by Priscilla Presley's memoir about Elvis's reliance on personal advisors. It's been covered by Johnny Cash.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the bluesy guitar riff — it was written after reading about Elvis's private lifelines.

name: Smalltown Boy (1984)
teaser: The song's synth-pop veneer hides a devastating story — a young gay man leaving his small town after being rejected by his family. The whistle and the final 'run away' became iconic.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the whistle at the end — it's the sound of leaving everything behind.

name: Relax (1983)
teaser: The BBC banned it over its suggestive lyrics, which only made it sell more — it was the UK's biggest-selling single of 1984. The song's relentless build made it a club legend.

exploreAction.targetName: Relax (1983) by Frankie Goes to Hollywood
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the tension that never fully releases — the whole song is a countdown to a chorus that keeps delaying.

name: West End Girls (1984)
teaser: The duo's spoken-rap verses and icy synth production made it a worldwide No. 1 — a song about class and the city. It's been called one of the best pop records ever made.

exploreAction.targetName: West End Girls (1984) by Pet Shop Boys
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the half-spoken verses — the song raps about London without ever calling itself rap.

name: It's a Sin (1987)
teaser: The song's guilt-ridden chorus was inspired by the duo's Catholic upbringing — 'everything I've ever done, forgive me'. The sweeping orchestral arrangement makes the guilt cinematic.

exploreAction.targetName: It's a Sin (1987) by Pet Shop Boys
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the strings and the church-organ feel — a confession booth turned into a dance record.

name: Money for Nothing (1985)
teaser: The lyric's famous 'I want my MTV' was sung by Sting as a guest vocal. The video was among the first to use computer-generated graphics, making it an MTV landmark.

exploreAction.targetName: Money for Nothing (1985) by Dire Straits
exploreAction.instruction: Listen for Sting's voice on the 'I want my MTV' line — he sang it as a favor and it became the song's hook.

name: Brothers in Arms (1985)
teaser: The song's anti-war theme was inspired by the Falklands conflict, and its slow, cinematic arrangement made it one of the decade's most moving records. The album was recorded with early digital technology.

exploreAction.targetName: Brothers in Arms (1985) by Dire Straits
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the quiet, resigned delivery — a war song that sounds like a funeral, not a battle.

name: With or Without You (1987)
teaser: The Edge's shimmering guitar — built on a delay effect — and Bono's desperate vocal made it U2's first US No. 1. The song was nearly cut from the album.

exploreAction.targetName: With or Without You (1987) by U2
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the Edge's guitar — it was created by accident with a delay pedal and became the song's whole mood.

name: I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For (1987)
teaser: The gospel-tinged spiritual search made it a global anthem. The band recorded it live in the studio with a gospel choir, and it became their second US No. 1.

exploreAction.targetName: I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For (1987) by U2
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the choir answering Bono — the song is a hymn that never finds its answer.

name: Where the Streets Have No Name (1987)
teaser: The band performed it on a rooftop in downtown LA for the video — the street below filled with onlookers and police. The song's slow-burning build became their live opener for years.

exploreAction.targetName: Where the Streets Have No Name (1987) by U2
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the guitar arpeggios that open the song — they were played on a rooftop in LA with police waiting below.

name: Pride (In the Name of Love) (1984)
teaser: It was written about Martin Luther King Jr. — the lyric famously says he was shot on April 4, and the band later corrected the mistaken date in live versions. The bassline drives the whole song.

exploreAction.targetName: Pride (In the Name of Love) (1984) by U2
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the driving bass — the song marches in honor of a man who led with nonviolence.

name: Sunday Bloody Sunday (1983)
teaser: It was written about the Bloody Sunday massacre in Northern Ireland, and Bono's opening — 'I can't believe the news today' — is a cry against violence. The martial drumbeat made it an anthem.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the military drumbeat — it's a protest march set to rock.

name: Eye of the Tiger (1982)
teaser: Rocky III's producers asked the band to write a theme after rejecting a Queen song — the result became one of the most motivating riffs in sports history. The band wrote it in a week.

exploreAction.targetName: Eye of the Tiger (1982) by Survivor
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the opening riff — it was written to make you want to run up stairs.

name: We Are the World (1985)
teaser: Michael Jackson and Lionel Richie wrote it for African famine relief, and the recording session gathered dozens of the era's biggest stars — from Bob Dylan to Bruce Springsteen. It became one of the best-selling singles ever.

exploreAction.targetName: We Are the World (1985) by USA for Africa
exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the superstar lineup — each singer takes a solo line, and the choir behind them is every star who wasn't soloing.

name: Do They Know It's Christmas? (1984)
teaser: The first charity supergroup single — Bob Geldof gathered British stars in a day to record it for Ethiopian famine relief. It was the UK's biggest-selling single at the time.

exploreAction.targetName: Do They Know It's Christmas? (1984) by Band Aid
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the famous opening — 'it's Christmastime' — and try to name all the voices in the group chorus.

name: In the Air Tonight (1981)
teaser: The drum fill near the end is one of the most famous in pop history — it was played live in the studio, and the song was built around a drum machine demo. The urban legend about it being about a drowning victim is false, but the legend persists.

exploreAction.targetName: In the Air Tonight (1981) by Phil Collins
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the drum fill at the end — Collins played it in one take on a live drum kit after a song of building tension.

name: Against All Odds (Take a Look at Me Now) (1984)
teaser: Written for the film of the same name, the ballad's raw vocal made it his first US No. 1. Collins later recorded a duet version with Marilyn Martin.

exploreAction.targetName: Against All Odds (Take a Look at Me Now) (1984) by Phil Collins
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the desperation in the chorus — the song is a plea, not a performance.

name: Beat It (1983)
teaser: The guitar solo was played by Eddie Van Halen, who came to the studio as a favor and recorded it in one take. The song's anti-gang message and its famous video made it a phenomenon.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the guitar solo — Eddie Van Halen recorded it for free, in one take, as a favor.

name: Bad (1987)
teaser: The title track's video was directed by Martin Scorsese, and the song's aggressive funk made it another record-breaking No. 1. Jackson wrote the lyric as a story about a kid who goes bad.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the funk bassline and the 'who's bad' call — a dance record with a threat in it.

name: Smooth Criminal (1987)
teaser: The song's famous anti-gravity lean was performed live with specially designed shoes that locked to the stage. The video, set in a 1930s speakeasy, made it iconic.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the heartbeat-like bass pulse — it's meant to sound like a racing pulse.

name: Man in the Mirror (1988)
teaser: The gospel-tinged ballad's message — change yourself to change the world — made it one of his most beloved records. The video montage of historical figures was groundbreaking.

exploreAction.targetName: Man in the Mirror (1988) by Michael Jackson
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the gospel choir building behind him — the song ends like a church service.

name: Wanna Be Startin' Somethin' (1983)
teaser: The 'ma ma se, ma ma sa' chant was borrowed from Manu Dibango's 'Soul Makossa' — a dispute that ended with Dibango receiving royalties. The song's relentless rhythm made it a dance classic.

exploreAction.targetName: Wanna Be Startin' Somethin' (1983) by Michael Jackson
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the African chant in the outro — it came from a Cameroonian saxophonist's hit.

name: Human Nature (1983)
teaser: It was written by Steve Porcaro of Toto, inspired by his daughter's phone calls — the 'why, why' refrain is her voice asking questions. It's one of Jackson's most delicate records.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the whispered 'why why' in the chorus — it was written about a little girl's phone questions.

name: Dancing in the Dark (1984)
teaser: The video featured a young Courtney Cox being pulled on stage to dance — one of MTV's most iconic moments. The song's synth-driven sound was a deliberate bid for radio play.

exploreAction.targetName: Dancing in the Dark (1984) by Bruce Springsteen
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the synth pulse under the rock — the Boss built it to be a hit, and it was.

name: Born in the U.S.A. (1984)
teaser: The anthemic chorus is often misread as patriotic, but the song is about a Vietnam veteran abandoned by his country. The synthesizer riff made it a global smash.

exploreAction.targetName: Born in the U.S.A. (1984) by Bruce Springsteen
exploreAction.instruction: Listen past the chorus — the verses tell a story of a veteran left with nothing.

name: Glory Days (1985)
teaser: The song about high-school glory fading became one of his biggest hits — the story of a pitcher who threw a 'speedball' at the school record. The video is full of playful cameos.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the driving guitar — the song is a celebration of stories told at a bar.

name: Faithfully (1983)
teaser: The band's piano ballad about life on the road — written by keyboardist Jonathan Cain about his own tour marriage — became one of their most enduring songs. It's a staple of power-ballad playlists.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the piano intro and the soaring chorus — a road life in four minutes.

name: Open Arms (1981)
teaser: The band's ballad was turned down by a producer who thought it was too soft — the band fought to keep it and it became one of their defining hits. It's been covered by Mariah Carey and many others.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to Steve Perry's high notes — the song almost got cut from the album.

name: Take My Breath Away (1986)
teaser: Written for Top Gun, the synth ballad won an Academy Award and became the sound of 80s romance. The band recorded it in one take with the lead singer feeling the scene.

exploreAction.targetName: Take My Breath Away (1986) by Berlin
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the drum machine and the breathless verses — the song was written to soundtrack a jet flying into a sunset.

name: 99 Luftballons (1983)
teaser: The German-language song about balloons mistaken for missiles on radar became an international hit — the band turned down offers to sing it in English. It's one of the few foreign-language songs to top US charts.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the story in the verses — 99 red balloons start a war that destroys everything.

name: Rock Me Amadeus (1985)
teaser: The rap-pop tribute to Mozart became the first German-language song to top the US charts. Falco's costume and the video's classical-meets-modern mashup made him a star.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the spoken verses — a rapper introducing Mozart as if he were a rock star.

name: Eat It (1984)
teaser: Al's parody of 'Beat It' became his breakthrough — Michael Jackson reportedly loved it and even let Al borrow the set from the 'Beat It' video. The song's rapid-fire parody verses are a comedy masterclass.

exploreAction.targetName: Eat It (1984) by Weird Al Yankovic
exploreAction.instruction: Listen for every detail the parody mimics — Al recreated the Beat It video's set with permission.

name: White Wedding (1982)
teaser: The song's guitar riff and its 'little sister' lyric made it an MTV staple — the video, with the biker wedding, defined 80s style. Idol wrote it about his sister's wedding.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the chant in the bridge — the song is a wedding invitation with a threat underneath.

name: Rebel Yell (1983)
teaser: The title came from a brand of whiskey shared with the Rolling Stones, and the song's relentless riff became Idol's signature. The video made him a global star.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the riff that never stops — the whole song is one long, defiant scream.

name: Eyes Without a Face (1984)
teaser: The song's eerie synth intro and its story of loss made it one of the most atmospheric hits of the decade. Idol wrote it after a relationship ended in tragedy.

exploreAction.targetName: Eyes Without a Face (1984) by Billy Idol
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the whispered, almost ghostly verses — the song is a ballad hiding inside a rock hit.

name: Burning Down the House (1983)
teaser: The band built the groove from a Parliament-Funkadelic jam, and the stuttering 'watch out' chorus became their biggest hit. The video, with the band performing in a burning room, is a classic.

exploreAction.targetName: Burning Down the House (1983) by Talking Heads
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the polyrhythm — the band wrote the groove by jamming to a funk record.

name: Once in a Lifetime (1980)
teaser: David Byrne's frantic spoken-sung delivery and the line 'same as it ever was' made it a meditation on modern life. The video, with Byrne's twitching dance, is one of the greatest ever made.

exploreAction.targetName: Once in a Lifetime (1980) by Talking Heads
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the preacher-like delivery — Byrne wrote it as a question about who we become without noticing.

name: Come On Eileen (1982)
teaser: The song's Celtic fiddle and the famous 'poor old Johnny Ray' opening made it one of the most beloved one-hit wonders — it topped the UK and US charts. The band's overalls in the video became iconic.

exploreAction.targetName: Come On Eileen (1982) by Dexys Midnight Runners
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the fiddle and the key change — the song swings between Irish folk and pop in one chorus.

name: Ghost Town (1981)
teaser: The ska band's eerie farewell — recorded during riots in British cities — was the first UK No. 1 of the 1980s. The song's haunting atmosphere predicted the decade's unrest.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the saxophone and the dread in the melody — a dance song that sounds like a town emptying out.

name: The Model (1981)
teaser: The synth-pop standard from Computer World was originally a B-side — it became a UK No. 1 after being re-released. Its icy, robotic precision influenced every electronic band that followed.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the mechanical precision — every note is quantized like a machine playing a fashion show.

name: Rio (1982)
teaser: The band recorded the video on a yacht in Antigua, launching the 'new romantic' visual style. The song's funky bassline and Nick Rhodes' synths made it a defining 80s record.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the bassline — it was written to match the yacht video's laid-back luxury.

name: Hungry Like the Wolf (1982)
teaser: The video — filmed in the Sri Lankan jungle — helped make Duran Duran MTV royalty. The song's exotic, percussive riff became their breakthrough.

exploreAction.targetName: Hungry Like the Wolf (1982) by Duran Duran
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the jungle percussion — the band recorded the video in a real rainforest.

name: True (1983)
teaser: The sophisti-pop ballad's famous line — 'I know this much is true' — was written by Gary Kemp in the style of soul music he loved. It became one of the decade's defining slow songs.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the sax and the smooth bassline — the song is a love letter to 60s soul, not to one person.

name: Down Under (1981)
teaser: The flute riff and the vegemite sandwich lyric made it an Australian anthem and a global No. 1. The song's travel-story verses were written by the band's frontman about touring.

exploreAction.targetName: Down Under (1981) by Men at Work
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the flute riff — it was written as a joke about Australian culture and became a worldwide hit.

name: The Safety Dance (1982)
teaser: The synth-pop hit was written about being told to stop dancing at a festival — the 'safety dance' was the dance you could do anywhere. It became an 80s one-hit wonder legend.

exploreAction.targetName: The Safety Dance (1982) by Men Without Hats
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the medieval-flavored synth melody — the song was a protest against rules against dancing.

name: Call Me (1980)
teaser: Written for the film American Gigolo, the song's disco-rock pulse became Blondie's biggest hit. It was the band's answer to a movie that needed a phone-call scene.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the driving bass and the disco strings — the song was written to soundtrack a phone call in a film.

name: Rapture (1980)
teaser: It was the first song with rapping to top the US charts — Debbie Harry's spoken verses name-dropped Fab Five Freddy and Grandmaster Flash. It brought hip-hop to mainstream radio.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the rap section in the middle — it was one of the first times mainstream radio heard hip-hop.

name: Under Pressure (1981)
teaser: The famous bassline was written by John Deacon — and it was later recycled by Vanilla Ice for 'Ice Ice Baby' without credit, leading to a settlement. The 'dum dum dum da da da' is one of pop's most recognized moments.

exploreAction.targetName: Under Pressure (1981) by Queen & David Bowie
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the bassline — it's been copied so many times you've heard it without knowing its origin.

name: Another One Bites the Dust (1980)
teaser: John Deacon wrote the bassline after hearing Chic — the funk influence was a departure for Queen. The song became their best-selling single ever.

exploreAction.targetName: Another One Bites the Dust (1980) by Queen
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the bassline — it was inspired by a disco record and became Queen's biggest seller.

name: I Want to Break Free (1984)
teaser: The video — with the band in drag parodying a soap opera — was banned in the US but beloved everywhere else. The song's themes of freedom made it a global anthem.

exploreAction.targetName: I Want to Break Free (1984) by Queen
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the synth bassline and the defiant chorus — the video's humor hides a serious message.

name: Radio Ga Ga (1984)
teaser: Written by Roger Taylor about the death of radio, the song's hand-wave chorus became a stadium ritual. It was inspired by Taylor's son saying 'radio ca-ca'.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the hand-clap beat — the audience wave that became a stadium tradition started at Queen shows.

name: Flashdance... What a Feeling (1983)
teaser: The Flashdance theme won an Oscar and a Grammy — its 'take your passion and make it happen' chorus became an anthem. Cara co-wrote the lyrics herself.

exploreAction.targetName: Flashdance... What a Feeling (1983) by Irene Cara
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the key change at the end — the song builds like the dance audition it scored.

name: Maniac (1983)
teaser: The Flashdance hit was originally written about a different kind of maniac entirely — the lyrics were rewritten for the film. The pulsing synth riff is unforgettable.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the frantic synth riff — it was composed for a different, darker song before the film rewrote it.

name: Ghostbusters (1984)
teaser: The theme's 'who you gonna call?' hook became a cultural phenomenon — and led to a lawsuit from Huey Lewis, who said it borrowed from 'I Want a New Drug'. Parker settled out of court.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the call-and-response chorus — the song is a radio ad for a fictional service.

name: Axel F (1984)
teaser: The Beverly Hills Cop theme's synth riff was created on a single synthesizer in a hotel room — it became one of the most recognizable instrumental hooks of the decade.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the synth riff — it was written on a portable keyboard in a hotel room.

name: Drive (1984)
teaser: The ballad's video told the story of a woman losing her memory — and its piano and Ric Ocasek's fragile vocal made it one of the decade's most moving records. It was the last song the band's bassist performed live before his death.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the piano and the stillness — a new wave band's most human moment.

name: Need You Tonight (1987)
teaser: The song's pulsing groove and Michael Hutchence's whispered verses were recorded in one take — it became the band's only US No. 1. The black-and-white video made them MTV stars.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the groove — the band recorded it live in the studio with the lights down.

name: Never Tear Us Apart (1988)
teaser: The band's most romantic song was written in a Prague studio after a night of drinking — the strings and the aching chorus made it their signature ballad.

exploreAction.targetName: Never Tear Us Apart (1988) by INXS
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the string section — it was recorded with a full orchestra in a cold Prague studio.

name: Beds Are Burning (1987)
teaser: The Australian band's protest song demanded the return of Aboriginal land — the video, filmed in the desert with the band shirtless, made the message unmissable. It became a worldwide hit.

exploreAction.targetName: Beds Are Burning (1987) by Midnight Oil
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the message in the chorus — the song is a legal claim set to a rock beat.

name: Owner of a Lonely Heart (1983)
teaser: It was the prog-rock band's only US No. 1 — built on a sample-heavy, funk-influenced sound that alienated old fans but conquered radio. The video's surreal imagery was groundbreaking.

exploreAction.targetName: Owner of a Lonely Heart (1983) by Yes
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the stuttering chorus — the band used a drum machine and samples for the first time.

name: In a Big Country (1983)
teaser: The band's signature was turning bagpipe-like guitar sounds into rock — Stuart Adamson played a guitar through an effects box to mimic Scottish pipes. The song became an anthem of wide-open spaces.

exploreAction.targetName: In a Big Country (1983) by Big Country
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the guitar pretending to be bagpipes — the band's whole sound is that trick.

name: Never Gonna Give You Up (1987)
teaser: The dance-pop classic became a worldwide meme decades later as the 'rickroll' — but it was a legitimate No. 1 hit first, with one of the decade's catchiest choruses. Astley has said he finds the meme hilarious.

exploreAction.targetName: Never Gonna Give You Up (1987) by Rick Astley
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the chorus — you know it from the meme, but this is the actual song that was a genuine hit.

name: Heaven Is a Place on Earth (1987)
teaser: The former Go-Go's frontwoman's solo smash made her a global star — the song's 'ooh baby, do you know what that's worth' chorus became instantly iconic. The video was filmed at a carnival.

exploreAction.targetName: Heaven Is a Place on Earth (1987) by Belinda Carlisle
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the key change before the final chorus — the song keeps lifting like a ride at the carnival.

name: Eternal Flame (1989)
teaser: The a cappella opening and the whispered verses made it one of the decade's most romantic records — it was written in an actual eternal flame exhibit at a cemetery. It was the band's last No. 1.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the a cappella intro — the song was written at a real eternal flame memorial.

name: Walk Like an Egyptian (1986)
teaser: The song's title and the video's jerky dance made it a worldwide phenomenon — it was written after the songwriter saw people imitating hieroglyphics. It became the band's biggest hit.

exploreAction.targetName: Walk Like an Egyptian (1986) by The Bangles
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the percussive, angular verses — the song makes your body move like the wall drawings it describes.

name: Manic Monday (1986)
teaser: It was written by Prince — he gave it to the band under a pseudonym as a favor. The song's 'wish it was Sunday' chorus became a Monday anthem everywhere.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the melody — it was written by Prince and handed to the band anonymously.

name: What's Love Got to Do with It (1984)
teaser: The song revived Tina Turner's career after a decade away — she reportedly disliked it at first. Its cool, dismissive delivery made it one of the defining records of the decade.

exploreAction.targetName: What's Love Got to Do with It (1984) by Tina Turner
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the detachment in her voice — the song is an argument against romance, delivered by a survivor.

name: Simply the Best (1989)
teaser: The anthem of commitment became her signature closer — and the song's title became a phrase used everywhere from sports to ads. Turner's live version is the definitive one.

exploreAction.targetName: Simply the Best (1989) by Tina Turner
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the way she attacks the chorus — the song is a promise made with full force.

name: Addicted to Love (1986)
teaser: The video — with Palmer flanked by identically dressed female musicians — became one of MTV's most parodied images. The song's crisp rock groove made it a worldwide hit.

exploreAction.targetName: Addicted to Love (1986) by Robert Palmer
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the tight rhythm section — the video's famous lineup was a comment on style over substance.

name: Alone (1987)
teaser: The power ballad's soaring vocal made it Heart's biggest hit — it was originally written for another band that passed on it. The song's key change is one of the most dramatic in pop.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the key change and Ann Wilson's sustained notes — the song was turned down by its first intended band.

name: The Final Countdown (1986)
teaser: The keyboard riff was written years before the song — it became one of the most recognizable (and parodied) openings in music. The band recorded it as a space-travel anthem.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the keyboard intro — it was a standalone riff that predated the song by years.

name: I Love Rock 'n' Roll (1981)
teaser: It's a cover of an obscure British band called the Arrows — Jett saw them on TV and recorded her version two years later. The riff became a rock radio staple.

exploreAction.targetName: I Love Rock 'n' Roll (1981) by Joan Jett & the Blackhearts
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the riff — it was written by a band that never charted; Jett's cover made it immortal.

name: Bad Reputation (1980)
teaser: The defiant anthem — 'I don't give a damn about my bad reputation' — became her signature after every label rejected her post-Runaways. She released it independently.

exploreAction.targetName: Bad Reputation (1980) by Joan Jett & the Blackhearts
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the sneer in the chorus — the song was recorded after every label turned her down.

name: Hit Me with Your Best Shot (1980)
teaser: The song's title is a boxing challenge, and its guitar riff became an arena staple. Benatar's powerful delivery made her one of MTV's first female rock stars.

exploreAction.targetName: Hit Me with Your Best Shot (1980) by Pat Benatar
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the guitar riff and the punchy chorus — the song is a dare.

name: Love Is a Battlefield (1983)
teaser: The song's dramatic key changes and the famous dance-choreography video made it one of the decade's biggest hits. The lyric came from the songwriter's own failed relationship.

exploreAction.targetName: Love Is a Battlefield (1983) by Pat Benatar
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the section where the beat drops to a whisper before exploding — the video's choreography was built around that moment.

name: Centerfold (1981)
teaser: The 'na na na na' chorus about discovering a high-school crush in a magazine made it their biggest hit. The song was written in minutes during a jam session.

exploreAction.targetName: Centerfold (1981) by The J. Geils Band
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the hand-claps and the na-na chorus — it was improvised in a rehearsal and kept.

name: Jessie's Girl (1981)
teaser: The song about wanting a friend's girlfriend was written while Springfield was filming a TV show — he jotted the title during a break. It became his only US No. 1.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the chorus's desperate confession — the whole song was born from a title scribbled between takes.

name: 867-5309/Jenny (1981)
teaser: The song made a fake phone number so famous that people actually tried calling it — and it's still a running joke. The 'Jenny' chorus became one of the decade's catchiest.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the number being sung over and over — real people called it for years, looking for Jenny.

name: Jack & Diane (1982)
teaser: The song about small-town teenagers — 'little ditty about Jack and Diane' — became his biggest hit. The title characters were inspired by a photograph Mellencamp saw.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the spoken intro — the song is a story about growing up in a town where nothing changes.

name: Sledgehammer (1986)
teaser: The stop-motion claymation video — full of dancing fruit and flying objects — won a record nine MTV awards. The song's horn section and Gabriel's grunts made it a worldwide hit.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the horn stabs and the bassline — and then find the video, which is a work of art on its own.

name: In Your Eyes (1986)
teaser: The song's famous sax solo and its use in the film Say Anything — the boombox scene — made it a love-song standard. Gabriel performed it live with Youssou N'Dour.

exploreAction.targetName: In Your Eyes (1986) by Peter Gabriel
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the sax at the end — it's the moment the boombox scene in Say Anything was built around.

name: Running Up That Hill (1985)
teaser: The song's theme is swapping places with a loved one to understand them — the title was chosen to make radio-friendly the real topic. It became a global hit again in 2022 when Stranger Things featured it.

exploreAction.targetName: Running Up That Hill (1985) by Kate Bush
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the Fairlight synth and the drum pattern — the song asks for a deal with God, then dances.

name: Love Will Tear Us Apart (1980)
teaser: The post-punk anthem was released weeks before singer Ian Curtis's death, giving its lyrics of failing love an unbearable weight. It's often called the greatest post-punk song ever.

exploreAction.targetName: Love Will Tear Us Apart (1980) by Joy Division
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the bassline and the melancholy — a song about a marriage falling apart, written by a man who didn't live to see it released.

name: A Forest (1980)
teaser: The band's atmospheric masterpiece uses a hypnotic bassline and Robert Smith's eerie guitar to tell a story of chasing someone into a forest. It's been a live staple for decades.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the bassline that never changes — the song is a walk deeper into the trees.

name: Just Like Heaven (1987)
teaser: The song's shimmering guitar arpeggios made it the band's most accessible hit — it was inspired by a trip to the beach with the woman he later married. The video is one of the decade's most loved.

exploreAction.targetName: Just Like Heaven (1987) by The Cure
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the guitar arpeggios — they were written after a beach day that became the song's story.

name: How Soon Is Now? (1984)
teaser: The song's famous tremolo guitar riff — copied from a Bo Diddley song and played on a cheap amp — made it an anthem of teenage isolation. It's been called the greatest Smiths song.

exploreAction.targetName: How Soon Is Now? (1984) by The Smiths
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the wah-wah tremolo — it was created by accident with a borrowed guitar and a cheap amplifier.

name: There Is a Light That Never Goes Out (1986)
teaser: Morrissey's lyric about wanting to die in a car crash with a loved one made it the band's most beloved song. The title has been borrowed by books, films and festivals.

exploreAction.targetName: There Is a Light That Never Goes Out (1986) by The Smiths
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the melancholy strings and the final, defiant chorus — the song turns death into romance.

name: This Charming Man (1983)
teaser: The band's first hit — with its jangling guitar and cryptic lyric about a bicycle accident — made them stars. It was recorded in two takes after the band had already finished the session.

exploreAction.targetName: This Charming Man (1983) by The Smiths
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the jangly guitar and the mysterious story — the song was recorded in minutes at the end of a session.

name: Losing My Religion (1991)
teaser: The song has no chorus in the traditional sense — Michael Stipe's repeated 'that's me in the corner' is the hook. The mandolin riff made it a global hit and a landmark music video.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the mandolin — the song's 'hook' isn't a chorus, it's a phrase repeated until it haunts.

name: Don't Look Back in Anger (1996)
teaser: The song's famous piano intro was lifted from John Lennon's 'Imagine' — Noel Gallagher admitted the borrowing freely. It's become one of Britain's most sung-along songs.

exploreAction.targetName: Don't Look Back in Anger (1996) by Oasis
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the piano intro — Gallagher says he copied it from 'Imagine' on purpose.

name: Champagne Supernova (1996)
teaser: The seven-minute closer of (What's the Story) Morning Glory? has a famously nonsensical chorus — Gallagher has called the lyrics 'complete gibberish'. It's still one of the band's most loved songs.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the long instrumental outro — the song drifts for minutes with no need to arrive anywhere.

name: Under the Bridge (1991)
teaser: Anthony Kiedis wrote the lyric as a poem about loneliness and addiction — the band nearly didn't record it because it was so personal. The song's gentle melody made them global stars.

exploreAction.targetName: Under the Bridge (1991) by Red Hot Chili Peppers
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the verses — a meditation on addiction and loneliness written as a private poem.

name: Give It Away (1991)
teaser: The song's funk-punk riff and Kiedis's mantra-like verses were inspired by a friend's advice to give everything away. It won the band their first Grammy.

exploreAction.targetName: Give It Away (1991) by Red Hot Chili Peppers
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the bassline and the stutter — the song is a funk sermon about letting go of things.

name: Scar Tissue (1999)
teaser: The song's slide guitar was played by John Frusciante, who co-wrote it as a reflection on his recovery from addiction. Its mellow, bruised feel marked a new chapter for the band.

exploreAction.targetName: Scar Tissue (1999) by Red Hot Chili Peppers
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the slide guitar — it was written by a guitarist writing about his own recovery.

name: Black (1991)
teaser: The band's manager convinced them to cut the song's explosive final chorus for the single, and Eddie Vedder has refused to play the full version live since 1994. It remains their most beloved song.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the quiet-loud structure — the single version fades before the song's true climax.

name: Even Flow (1991)
teaser: The song's famous guitar solo was improvised in the studio in one take. Its title — 'even flow' — came from the phrase Eddie Vedder heard in a therapist's office.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the solo — it was improvised in a single take and kept.

name: Alive (1991)
teaser: The song's story — a mother seeing her son as her dead husband — is actually the first part of a three-song story Vedder wrote. It became the anthem that launched the band.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the outro solo — the song's story continues in two other Pearl Jam songs.

name: Jeremy (1991)
teaser: The song was inspired by the true story of a Texas student who shot himself in front of his class. The band pulled the video after it aired due to its graphic ending.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the building anger — the song tells a real tragedy from the inside.

name: Man in the Box (1990)
teaser: The song's crushing riff and Layne Staley's howl made it a grunge landmark. The 'box' of the title is the coffin of addiction.

exploreAction.targetName: Man in the Box (1990) by Alice in Chains
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the howl at the end of the chorus — the song is about the trap of dependence.

name: Would? (1992)
teaser: Written about the death of a friend from overdose, the song's sludgy riff and eerie harmonies became the band's signature. It appeared on the Singles soundtrack.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the close harmonies over the doom-metal riff — grief and sludge together.

name: Rooster (1992)
teaser: Jerry Cantrell wrote it about his father's service in the Vietnam War — 'rooster' was his dad's nickname. The song became one of the band's most powerful.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the slow-burning verses — a son writing about his father's war.

name: Black Hole Sun (1994)
teaser: The song's surreal title was inspired by a news report Chris Cornell heard — and the video's melting faces became one of MTV's most famous. It won the band a Grammy.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the dreamlike melody — the title came from a news phrase Cornell misheard and kept.

name: Spoonman (1994)
teaser: The song began as a theme for a real Seattle street performer who played spoons. The percussion at the end includes actual spoon playing recorded live.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen for the spoons — the song was written for a real spoon-playing street musician.

name: Heart-Shaped Box (1993)
teaser: The song's title came from a box of chocolates shaped like a heart Kurt Cobain saw — and the video's dark imagery made it one of the decade's most talked-about. It was one of the last Nirvana singles.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the dynamics — the song snaps between whisper and scream like the artwork it inspired.

name: Lithium (1991)
teaser: Cobain's lyric about finding religion as a crutch — 'I'm so happy 'cause today I've found my friends' — shows his love of irony. The song's sudden shifts were the blueprint for grunge.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to how violently the song switches between calm verses and screaming choruses.

name: Come as You Are (1991)
teaser: The song's famous riff is nearly identical to Killing Joke's 'Eighties' — the band sued and settled out of court. Its gentle verses made it Nirvana's accessible side.

exploreAction.targetName: Come as You Are (1991) by Nirvana
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the riff — it's almost the same as a Killing Joke song, and the lawsuit was settled quietly.

name: Song 2 (1997)
teaser: The band recorded the 2-minute blast as a joke on American grunge — the 'woo-hoo' chant made it a global hit anyway. It's become a stadium and sports anthem.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the woo-hoo — the song was written as a parody of loud American rock.

name: Girls & Boys (1994)
teaser: The song's disco-punk groove and its lyric about holiday romance made it a UK sensation — the video, full of cheap seaside glamour, defined the Britpop era's look.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the bassline and the spoken verses — a critique of party culture that became a party anthem.

name: Parklife (1994)
teaser: The song's spoken verses were delivered by actor Phil Daniels, giving the album its east-London voice. It's one of the most British songs ever recorded.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the spoken-word verses — the song is narrated by a character, not the singer.

name: Common People (1995)
teaser: Jarvis Cocker's story of a rich student wanting to live like the working class became Britpop's sharpest social commentary. The song's monologue and its disco build made it an anthem.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the story in the verses — it's a class war conducted over a disco beat.

name: Disco 2000 (1995)
teaser: The song is a memory of a childhood crush — 'we were born within one hour of each other'. The disco groove made it one of the decade's biggest UK hits.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the chorus's counting — the song is a reunion fantasy that never quite happens.

name: There She Goes (1990)
teaser: The jangly guitar song was famously mistaken for a love song — it's actually about heroin addiction. The band recorded it dozens of times before settling on the released version.

exploreAction.targetName: There She Goes (1990) by The La's
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the sweetness — the song's subject is a drug, not a person.

name: Alright (1995)
teaser: The band's joyful two-minute blast — with its school-uniform video — captured 90s optimism. The 'we are young' chant made it an eternal summer anthem.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the sprint of it — the whole song is under three minutes of pure momentum.

name: Tubthumping (1997)
teaser: The band was known for political punk before this accidental global hit — 'I get knocked down, but I get up again' became a sports and meme staple. The band gave the profits to charity and protest groups.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the pub-chant chorus — a protest band's surprise worldwide smash.

name: Bittersweet Symphony (1997)
teaser: The song's string riff was sampled from an orchestral version of a Rolling Stones song — a legal battle left the band without royalties for years. It became one of the decade's defining songs anyway.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the strings — the sample's legal fight meant the band lost the rights to their own biggest hit.

name: The Drugs Don't Work (1997)
teaser: Richard Ashcroft wrote it about his father's illness — the lyric's plea became one of the most heartbreaking choruses of the decade. It was the band's only UK No. 1.

exploreAction.targetName: The Drugs Don't Work (1997) by The Verve
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the resignation in the chorus — a song about watching someone fade.

name: Teenage Dirtbag (2000)
teaser: The song's high-school revenge story became a global hit in 2000 — the 'her name is Noelle' chorus made it an anthem for every kid who didn't fit in. It took years to chart after being written.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the story — the narrator's crush ends up having a brother who's a fan.

name: Loser (1993)
teaser: The song was written in minutes with a drummer friend — Beck raps 'I'm a loser baby' over a beat borrowed from a rap record. It made him an accidental slacker-rock star.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the slacker drawl — the song was improvised in a single afternoon.

name: Where It's At (1996)
teaser: The song's mantra — 'I've got two turntables and a microphone' — became a catchphrase. It won a Grammy for Best Male Rock Vocal.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the turntable scratches and the spoken parts — the song is a love letter to DJ culture.

name: Sabotage (1994)
teaser: The song's frantic riff and the video — a parody of 70s cop-show openings — made it a cultural landmark. It's one of the most famous videos of the decade.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the bass-led chaos — the video's fake cop show was so convincing some thought it was real.

name: Intergalactic (1998)
teaser: The video — with giant robots fighting in a city — became one of the most famous of the decade. The song's goofy monster-rap chorus made it a worldwide hit.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the robot growls and the bass — the video's giant robots were designed by the band.

name: California Love (1995)
teaser: The West Coast anthem was built on a synth line sampled from Joe Cocker — and it became one of the biggest rap records ever. The video, set in a Mad Max-style California, was a landmark.

exploreAction.targetName: California Love (1995) by 2Pac feat. Dr. Dre
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the opening — a message from a future California before the beat drops.

name: Gin and Juice (1993)
teaser: The laid-back G-funk classic was written and recorded in a single night. Snoop's effortless flow made it one of the defining rap records of the decade.

exploreAction.targetName: Gin and Juice (1993) by Snoop Dogg

name: Nuthin' but a 'G' Thang (1992)

exploreAction.targetName: Nuthin' but a 'G' Thang (1992) by Dr. Dre feat. Snoop Dogg
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the sample of Leon Haywood's 'I Want'a Do Something Freaky to You' — it's the whole groove.

name: Regulate (1994)

exploreAction.targetName: Regulate (1994) by Warren G feat. Nate Dogg
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the two verses — the song is actually two separate stories cut together.

name: It Was a Good Day (1992)

exploreAction.targetName: It Was a Good Day (1992) by Ice Cube
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the ending — the whole 'good day' turns out to be a dream.

name: Jump Around (1992)
teaser: The song's relentless horn loop made it an instant party classic — it's still played at nearly every sports stadium. The band's rapper, Everlast, later reinvented himself as a blues artist.

exploreAction.targetName: Jump Around (1992) by House of Pain
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the horn sample — the song has been a stadium anthem for three decades.

name: C.R.E.A.M. (1993)
teaser: The song's chorus — 'cash rules everything around me' — became one of hip-hop's most quoted lines. The piano loop, sampled from a 60s soul record, is legendary.

exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the piano loop — a 60s soul sample that became hip-hop's most quoted money anthem.

name: N.Y. State of Mind (1994)
teaser: The opening track of Illmatic — produced by DJ Premier — set the standard for New York rap with its dense, literary verses. It's often ranked among the greatest rap songs ever.

exploreAction.targetName: N.Y. State of Mind (1994) by Nas
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the drum break and the imagery — a song so dense it rewards ten listens.

name: Big Poppa (1994)
teaser: The song's smooth, seductive flow over an Isaac Hayes sample made it Biggie's breakout hit. It turned the hardest rapper in New York into a ladies' man.

exploreAction.targetName: Big Poppa (1994) by The Notorious B.I.G.
exploreAction.instruction: Listen to the Isaac Hayes sample and the relaxed delivery — a gangster record designed to seduce.

name: Juicy (1994)
